article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Prestige International Pictures (PIP) has acquired all sales rights to SXSW Midnighters title Fifteen ( Quince ), outside of Latin America, ahead of the AFM in November.

Taking its cue from the Latin American tradition of quinceañera, a coming-of-age celebration when a girl turns 15, the film was directed by Mexican brothers Jack Zagha and Yossy Zagha from an original screenplay by Andrzej Rattinger and Ricardo Álvarez Canales ( (100 Days to Fall in Love) .

Related Stories

Top 50 Classic Horror Movies

Top 50 Halloween Movies Photo Gallery: Creepy Classics From ‘Psycho,’ ‘The Shining’ To ‘Obsession’ & ‘Get Out’

Since its premiere at SXSW, it has played a raft of international genre and film festivals, including Seattle, Fantaspoa and Neuchâtel.

The body horror follows a Mexican girl who has been planning the perfect quinceañera with her best friend until she begins to transform into something monstrous, causing a rift in their friendship as her birthday party spirals into chaos.

Watch on Deadline

Greta Martí stars alongside Macarena Oz (Nadie nos va a extrañar) , Aminta Ireta, Cloe Furlong and Mercedes Hernández, who recently appeared in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger .

The film was produced by the Zagha bothers for Avanti Pictures alongside Elsa Reyes and Películas V’s Valentín Javier Diment and Vanesa Pagani. The Mexican and Argentine co-production was made with the support and participation of the Mexican Film Institute (IMCINE), through FIDECINE, FOCINE and EFICINE.

“People keep telling teenage girls, ‘You’re becoming a woman,’ as if that isn’t terrifying enough,” said Yossy Zagha. “We took that fear and put it inside the biggest party of her life.

“I’m thrilled to invite buyers at AFM to this gory quinceañera if they dare to attend,” said Prestige president Carlos Rincon. “Jack and Yossy have crafted a supernatural coming-of-age horror that draws on familiar elements of classics such as Carrie and Rosemary’s Baby but with a Mexican twist.”

Prestige president Carlos Rincon negotiated the deal with producers Jack and Yossy Zagha.

article_text:
Films and events

Cult

Hot Spot

The new film from the acclaimed director of The Silent Twins is a daring and distinctive sci-fi thriller set in a near-future society ruled by sentient AI.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Agnieszka Smoczyńska

Screenwriter Robert Bolesto

With Andrzej Konopka, Noomi Rapace, Reika Kirishima

Poland-Greece 2026. 101min

Courtesy of Focus Features

Languages English, Japanese, Polish With some English subtitles

Access information

Saturday 10 October 21:00

Audio description

Monday 12 October 18:00

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Thursday 15 October 13:30

Audio description

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Djonny, a vibrantly dressed private eye, is called to solve a mysterious murder case, only to discover a rebel group capable of undermining the digital overlord led by Rana, who may or may not be a cyber witch. Agnieszka Smoczyńska creates a hypnotic, dystopian world that lures you in with its breathtaking aesthetics and hallucinatory images.

Isabel Moir

Content advice

Contains flashing images.

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury and nudity.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Too Many Beasts

In this deliciously unhinged mash-up of rural thriller and dark comedy, enormous wild boars create havoc in a small French town.

Tropical Fractals

Leonardo Pirondi’s timely reflection on ecological collapse imagines a future in which a biodome spaceship preserves the last traces of life on Earth.

Chronovisor

The film collective Cosmic Salon (Jack Auen and Kevin Walker) make their beguiling and assured feature debut, guiding us through hidden histories and uncanny landscapes of belief, mystery and the unknown.

article_text:
As Jamie Dornan visits Middle-earth for his next role, he’s not attempting to fill Viggo Mortensen ‘s boots for The Lord of the Rings : The Hunt for Gollum .

The Golden Globe nominee, who takes on the role of Aragorn for the upcoming Andy Serkis-helmed prequel, opened up about the “pressure” of playing the J.R.R. Tolkien character, explaining that for him, the role “will always be just Viggo” after Mortensen originated him in 2001’s The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring .

“There’s pressure when you’re trying to follow in those footsteps,” he admitted to L’Officiel . “I’ve been asked to play a super-iconic role, and I’ll do my best.”

Related Stories

‘The Lord Of The Rings: The Hunt For Gollum’: Jamie Dornan And Leo Woodall Join Film – CinemaCon

‘The Lord Of The Rings: The Hunt For Gollum’: Everything We Know So Far

Dornan continued, “But for me, Aragorn will always be just Viggo. His performance is one of my all-time favorites, and I feel honored to try to recapture at least some of the energy he originally brought to the character. There’s no part of me that’s trying to outdo him.”

Watch on Deadline

At CinemaCon in April, Warner Bros. announced that Dorman will play Strider (an alias for Aragorn) in the movie, which is set for a Dec. 17, 2027 release. The announcement also included Leo Woodall’s casting as Halvard.

A return to New Line’s Middle-earth franchise, which is based on the works of Tolkien, The Hunt for Gollum follows Aragorn’s perilous quest to capture Gollum before the creature can reveal the Ring’s location to Sauron. The story, much of it developed from Tolkien’s footnotes, is set between the events of The Hobbit and The Fellowship of the Ring .

Serkis, who is directing, will reprise his role of Gollum, with Elijah Wood and Ian McKellen returning as Frodo and Gandalf. Lee Pace is also back as Thranduil. Deadline previously reported that Kate Winslet will be joining the film in the role of Marigol.

Overton）等到他去世后再为他写传记；近十年后问世的成果敏锐、富有启发性，且本身就是一部美学杰作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "结合钱内尔·舍韦勒·拉塞尔（Channelle Chevelle Russell）对曼哈顿高古轩画廊迪娜·劳森（Deana Berger himself had asked the novelist Tom Overton to wait until his death to write his biography; arriving nearly a decade after, the result is perceptive, illuminating, and an aesthetic work in its own right."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s good reading when paired with Channelle Chevelle Russell’s review of an exhibition of Deana Lawson’s photographs at Gagosian Gallery in Manhattan. Lawson turns her camera’s gaze to beauty-supply surveillance photos of customers, which are often pinned behind the counter to deter theft. The gallery does not allow visitors to take photographs of the exhibition."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The resulting questions are deeply Bergerian, if I may: Who gets to look? Who gets looked at? Who has the power to determine what an image means?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/51/f8/51f871d8-b6be-4a73-b958-0ca4fff0110a/content/images/2026/10/john-berger.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Hyperallergic"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "John Berger in His Own Bruised Time", "links": [{"text": "John Berger in His Own Bruised Time", "url": "https://hyperallergic.com/john-berger-in-his-own-bruised-time/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These days, we tend to take his ideas for granted: that art — making it or contemplating it — creates knowledge. That by foregrounding the processes by which we see, we can discover the mechanisms and deceptions through which we make meaning. And, of course, that it’s important to know who is footing the bill. John Berger, who died in 2017, was famous not for challenging the Western canon but for making its revelations feel so evidently connected to everything else about life. Daily Newsletter

Seeing Like John Berger

Megan O’Grady reviews a new Berger biography, Deana Lawson appropriates surveillance photographs, and Paddy Johnson answers the question: Do I need an agent?

The writer and critic John Berger — that “anarchist-angel,” as essayist Megan O’Grady calls him in a review of his new biography — very much shaped the way we see. Berger himself had asked the novelist Tom Overton to wait until his death to write his biography; arriving nearly a decade after, the result is perceptive, illuminating, and an aesthetic work in its own right.

It’s good reading when paired with Channelle Chevelle Russell’s review of an exhibition of Deana Lawson’s photographs at Gagosian Gallery in Manhattan. Lawson turns her camera’s gaze to beauty-supply surveillance photos of customers, which are often pinned behind the counter to deter theft. The gallery does not allow visitors to take photographs of the exhibition.

The resulting questions are deeply Bergerian, if I may: Who gets to look? Who gets looked at? Who has the power to determine what an image means?

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

John Berger in His Own Bruised Time

These days, we tend to take his ideas for granted: that art — making it or contemplating it — creates knowledge. That by foregrounding the processes by which we see, we can discover the mechanisms and deceptions through which we make meaning. And, of course, that it’s important to know who is footing the bill. John Berger, who died in 2017, was famous not for challenging the Western canon but for making its revelations feel so evidently connected to everything else about life. His essays often read like personal letters, offering to us the gift of our own passions and imaginations. | Megan O’Grady

A Magnetizing Force: Salvaged Metal Meets Colorful Paint Skin

American artist Kennedy Yanko’s first-ever institutional solo exhibition in Paris opens on October 15, 2026, at the Cité de l’architecture et du patrimoine. Curated by Matthieu Poirier, Ce qui nous rassemble , which translates to “That which unites us” in English, engages Yanko’s contemporary sculptures in dialogue with a charged architectural history.

Actor Johnny Depp gets his first major exhibition in the UK at London’s Halcyon Gallery, despite the debatable quality of his work. [ Deadline ]

Curated by Mia Lopez, 16 artists transform everyday objects into bold explorations of Latinx identity. On view in San Antonio from October 16 through March 7, 2027.

article_text:
Much has been written on the new dating politics practiced by Gen-Z — more progressive socially, more conservative sexually, if you believe the hot takes, which you probably shouldn’t. Either way, that sensibility has yet to trickle down to mainstream portrayals of Zoomer romance on screen, which remain largely beholden to templates established by previous generations. “ Love Language ” is the latest in a line of youthful romantic comedies in nostalgic thrall to ’90s tropes of the genre, from klutzy meet-cutes to gay best friends to climactic airport interventions, and if it modestly updates proceedings with queer marriage and cocaine jokes, it still suggests that our species’ mating rituals have largely held fast. That Joey Power ‘s palatable, attractively assembled film will likely be a comfort watch for many under-30s should in turn be a comfort to their elders.

Related Stories

‘12.12: The Day’ Director Kim Sung-soo Says AI ‘Shows What’s in Your Imagination’

Like many latter-day romcoms, “Love Language” is cozily, even sentimentally romantic, while neglecting the comic half of the equation — despite a premise with ample potential for wit. Chloë Grace Moretz stars as Louisa, an allegedly gifted but perennially blocked writer who chances into an unexpectedly lucrative side hustle penning other people’s wedding vows, all while struggling to articulate her own messy romantic feelings for two different men. It’s a solid setup, but Power (who last directed the 2018 romance “After Everything,” starring Jeremy Allen White and Maika Monroe) isn’t the best with words himself: The film coasts off the combined charms of its ensemble and location, with Chicago shot in warm, perma-autumnal tones, and thus goes down quite easily. It would be nice, though, if it was funny too.

Popular on Variety

Well, you can’t have everything — as a jaded Louisa, recently burned by a broken-off engagement, is wont to think. Her broken heart makes her something of a killjoy at the bachelorette party of her best friend Tilda (Billie Lourd), but does present an upside for the bride-to-be: When Tilda asks Louisa to help with her wedding vows, Louisa merely repurposes those she had written for her own aborted nuptials. Her style may be a bit “Hallmark × Rupi Kaur” but the vows go down a treat, and when word gets out at the wedding that Louisa ghostwrote them, total strangers approach her to request their own dewy-eyed dedications. It’s a productive wedding all round: She also meets Tilda’s sexy cousin Dash (a terrific Anthony Ramos ), and though she’s a little thrown by his straight-talking manner, there’s clearly a spark between them.

She’s quickly distracted, however, when she’s commissioned by wealthy importer Olivia (Isabel May) to write her vows for her upcoming wedding to dreamboat public defender Warren ( Manny Jacinto ) — who, it turns out, is Louisa’s old college crush. Taking the job while keeping that fact from Olivia, she finds old feelings rekindled as she spends more time with the couple; at the same time, she casually dates Dash, but discourages his more serious advances. And as Olivia and Warren’s big day draws nearer, she finds herself unable to write a word.

It’s a romantic quadrangle in which the two most storied individuals are also the least interesting. Moretz capably juggles Louisa’s neuroses and delusions, not shying from the character’s tendency toward selfishness and self-pity, but it’s May’s Olivia, cannily played as both a princess and an underestimated observer, whom we want to know better. And while we’re treated to multiple scenes of Louisa and Warren hanging out and fondly reflecting on old times, he’s not half as charismatic or ultimately soul-baring as Dash is — which makes her romantic dilemma feel overly protracted and low-stakes, evading the emotional complexities of an evenly weighted choice. (The premise is plainly a nod to the likewise Chicago-set genre standard “My Best Friend’s Wedding,” though the beauty of that film is that it presented Julia Roberts’ protagonist with altogether less enviable options: homewrecking or continued singledom.)

Perhaps the script is unduly tilted by Ramos’ drawling, sincerely beguiling delivery. Handed a fairly two-dimensional character concept — fuckboi with a nesting impulse — he crafts a personality that feels more embedded in the real world than everyone else here. Moretz’s performance, too, is livelier and more limber in his presence; away from him, Louisa feels a bit floatily conceived. Her day job (as a WFH copywriter), friendships (including with Lukas Gage’s gay lothario turned broody plot device) and even her apartment want for detail and texture, as “Love Language” largely colors its story with allusions to other movies and pop ephemera. It’s a pleasant, undemanding watch in large part because it’s all so very recognizable, but one wonders when a more generationally defining romcom will come along.

article_text:
The box office success of “ La Bola Negra ,” handled by Elastica Films, has given Spain’s independent film distribution sector a timely boost. The momentum comes as Valladolid’s Merci market enters its sixth edition, its first since the death of José Luis Cienfuegos, the director of Valladolid, known in Spain as the Seminci , who helped build the event.

Running Oct. 28-30 at Valladolid’s Broadway cinemas, Merci looks set to draw more than 200 industry professionals. Its 26-film slate gives exhibitors an advance look at releases scheduled for late 2026 and the first half of 2027.

Organized by Valladolid and Adicine , whose 20 member companies account for the vast majority of Spain’s independent film distribution sector, Merci brings distributors and exhibitors together to discuss release strategies, present marketing campaigns and forge business ties.

Popular on Variety

At last October’s Merci, Comscore reported that Adicine members had captured a 12% share of Spain’s theatrical box office through September 2025. Following the runaway success of “La Bola Negra” — now Spain’s fourth highest-grossing domestic film ever, with more than €29.9 million ($33.5 million) and counting — that share could reach 16%-20% by year-end, estimates Adicine co-president Enrique Costa, Elastica Films co-founder.

“‘La Bola Negra’ shows that independent distributors can handle major Spanish films with mainstream appeal and deliver exceptional results,” Costa says.

Other recent successes range from Spanish films “Sundays” and “Sirât,” both distributed by BTeam Pictures, to international titles “Sentimental Value” and “Backrooms,” handled by Elastica.

Winning Over Exhibitors

Merci 2026’s lineup features Gerardo Herrero’s buzzy war thriller “Carta Blanca,” from Karma Films; Javier Ruiz Caldera’s San Sebastián Fest comedy hit “5 More Minutes,” which has just closed a major sale handled in and ouside Spain by Filmax; and Florian Zeller’s “Bunker,” starring Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem, co-produced by MOD Producciones and distributed locally by Elastica.

Among the international highlights are Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Fjord,” from Caramel Films and Filmin, and Beth de Araújo’s Sundance prizewinner “Josephine,” starring Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan, handled by A Contracorriente Films.

Beyond showcasing their upcoming releases, distributors want to persuade exhibitors to give independent films the support they need in theaters. Costa urges cinema operators to “program, nurture and protect” those films. “It’s about finding allies,” he says.

Successful releases are already helping build confidence between the two sides of the business.

“Exhibitors know which distributors have delivered successful releases, and that gives them confidence in what those companies bring next,” says Adicine co-president Lara Pérez-Camiña.

Merci also serves as “a barometer,” Pérez-Camiña says, allowing distributors to gauge exhibitors’ reactions to upcoming releases.

The association’s companies handle everything from Spanish auteur films with crossover ambitions to international arthouse releases and commercially oriented genre fare.

For smaller distributors, Merci effectively doubles as an exhibitor convention they could scarcely afford to organize on their own.

“There are many films that, without Merci, might have found it harder to secure support from cinemas or television buyers,” Pérez-Camiña says.

Movistar Plus, Filmin and HBO are among the streaming platforms Pérez-Camiña identifies as regular Merci participants and key buyers of independent films.

A Market in Transition

The sixth edition is also Merci’s first without Cienfuegos, who played a central role in shaping the market. The festival’s new leadership, Javier H. Estrada and Mariona Viader, has maintained its collaboration with Adicine.

“We’ve felt very supported by the festival’s new management from the outset,” Costa says. He points to this year’s increased participation as evidence of continuing industry interest.

Merci will honor Golem distribution and exhibition veteran Otilio García with the newly named José Luis Cienfuegos Award for professional achievement, to be presented Oct. 29.

Beyond the Screening Room

The professional program will explore new ways to attract moviegoers through the panel “Cinemas, Distributors and Platforms: Together for Audiences.”

The discussion will offer an opportunity to address theatrical windows. Independent distributors, Costa argues, “continue to maintain longer windows” than other distributors, something he believes exhibitors should take into account.

Mark de Quervain of Eventive will lead a presentation titled “License to Discover: AI, Agentic Search and Cinema’s Next Audience,” in collaboration with Europa Cinemas. Another session, “Towards Accessible Cinema With Greta App,” will examine accessibility for moviegoers.

Rentrak Spain will present box office trends and fresh findings from Cinequest, an audience research tool launched by Comscore in 2025.

Running alongside Merci on Oct. 29-30, Seminci’s La Meseta Distribution Lab will showcase seven independent feature film release campaigns developed with industry mentors. The campaigns will compete for awards totaling $10,500, to be presented at Merci’s Oct. 30 closing ceremony.

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "1591 年 3 月。聚楽第。 20 歳をちょっと過ぎたばかりの４人の青年が、太閤秀吉の前でヨーロッパの楽器を奏でた。演奏された楽器は、クラヴォ（小型の鍵盤楽器）、小型のハープ、リュート、ラベキーニャ（小型のヴァイオリンのような弦楽器）。秀吉は彼らの演奏を大変気に入り、３度にわたってアンコールを所望したという。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/db368644b793d7e5960eb572220b72df.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "豊臣秀吉像（秀吉生誕地名古屋・常泉寺）", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "青年たちは、九州のキリシタン大名たちの名代としてヨーロッパに派遣された日本初の公的な外国訪問団「天正遣欧少年使節」のメンバーである。実際に演奏された曲は不明だが、音楽史家の故皆川達夫氏は、ルネッサンス音楽の大家ジョスカン・デプレの名曲で、ヨーロッパで大人気だったシャンソン「千々の悲しみ」を候補曲として挙げている。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "実際、青年たちの腕前は確かだったらしい。出発前には日本の神学校で楽器を学び、旅の間も寄港地で練習に励んだ。ポルトガルのエヴォラの街では、使節の２人が大司教の要望に応じて大聖堂のオルガンで見事な腕前を披露し、一同の喝采を受けたという。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「天正遣欧少年使節」もまた、前回この連載で触れた「対抗宗教改革」の賜物である。プロテスタントの攻勢に対抗するべく世界への布教に乗り出したカトリック勢力が、日本におけるさらなる布教に対する援助を目的に、キリシタン大名とつながりがあり（実際は必ずしもそうではなかったが）模範的な日本の少年信者をヨーロッパへ派遣したのが「天正少年遣欧使節」だ。さまざまな困難に遭遇しながらヨーロッパに到着した一行は、行く先々で大歓迎を受けた。それはカトリック教会にとっては自分たちが地の果てまで浸透した証であり、日本にとってはその存在が証明された出来事となった。"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "フェリペ２世に謁見した少年使節"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "少年たちの最終目的地はもちろんヴァチカンだったが、ヴァチカン訪問の前年、 1584 年に、彼らはヨーロッパ一の権力者の謁見にあずかっている。スペイン国王、フェリペ２世である。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/b6751ad76411c12d5dc7aabc93c9259a-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "ティツィアーノ「鎧を着たフェリペ2世の肖像」1551年", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ハプスブルク家が 16 世紀に「太陽の沈むことがない（常に領土のどこかで太陽が輝いている）」大帝国へと発展したのは、第３回でご紹介したマクシミリアン 1 世の子供たちがスペイン王家と縁組したからである。マクシミリアンの孫カール５世（神聖ローマ皇帝）はスペイン王カルロス１世を兼ね、その子の代でハプスブルク家はスペイン系とオーストリア系に分かれたが、スペイン国王となったフェリペ２世は在位中にポルトガルを併合、また新大陸やアジアに植民地を獲得して大帝国の盟主となった。"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "歴史的には「悪役」のイメージ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "だが歴史上の位置付けでは、フェリペ２世は悪役である。フェリペはオーストリアのハプスブルク家以上に、「対抗宗教改革」のリーダーとして権勢を振るった。「異端者が入り込むくらいなら領土を失い、１００回死んだ方がまし」とまで発言し、プロテスタントにとどまらずユダヤ教やイスラム教からの改宗者にも目を光らせ、少しでも疑わしければ捕らえて拷問にかけ、時には処刑した。「異端者火刑」は大いなる見せ物でもあった。その様子はヴェルディのオペラ《ドン・カルロス》で垣間見ることができる。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "近年、フェリペ治下での異端審問が従来言われていたほど厳しくなかったという研究が出てきたが、彼の弾圧に反発して、オランダが独立戦争に突入したのは史実である。その結果フェリペは、マクシミリアン以来帝国の一部だった、最も富裕な領土を失ったのだった。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "日本における布教を牽引したイエズス会もスペインの組織であり、少年使節がフェリペを表敬訪問するのは当然だった。宮殿と礼拝堂を兼ねた大建築であるエル・エスコリアル宮殿で彼らに謁見したフェリペは喜び、少年たちと一緒にミサに参列している。フェリペの宮廷には立派な宮廷楽団があり、信心深い国王のため、壮麗な典礼音楽が演奏されていた。少年たちが聴いたのは、当代を代表する宗教音楽の大家、トマス・ルイス・デ・ビクトリアの音楽だったかもしれない。"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "スペイン王室でも音楽を重要視"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "オーストリア・ハプスブルク家同様、スペイン・ハプスブルク家の音楽組織もインターナショナルだった。フェリペの父カールは、ニコラ・ゴンベールをはじめとするフランドルの有名な音楽家をスペインに連れてきた。フェリペの母ファナの一族であるスペイン宮廷でも音楽は盛んで、ラテン語の教会音楽に加え、スペイン語の歌も歌われていた。カールの代に二つの楽団は合併し、帝国の富を背景に、ヨーロッパ随一の王室礼拝堂楽団が出来上がった。ちなみに皆川氏が秀吉の御前演奏の曲の候補として挙げている「千々の悲しみ」は、カール５世が愛好し、「皇帝の歌」と呼ばれた曲である。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "フェリペ自身もヴィエラという楽器を弾くなど多少音楽は嗜んだが、夢中になるというほどではなかったようだ。それよりも音楽は、日々のミサや年中行事を通じて、やはり王室の権威を表すプロパガンダとして用いられた。カールとフェリペの２代に仕えた有名な音楽家に、盲目のオルガニスト、アントニオ・デ・カベソンがいるが、フェリペはフランドルのオルガン製作者ジル・ブレヴォスに、エル・エスコリアルの礼拝堂に大オルガンを建造させている。天正少年使節もまた、巨大な大聖堂を満たす華麗な音響に震え上がったのではないだろうか。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/08e67bccbcbeda6dc31516e4ead4aada-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "エル・エスコリアル", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "美術にも情熱を傾けたフェリペ２世"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
秀吉が３度アンコールを求めた西洋音楽

今年の大河ドラマ「豊臣兄弟！」でも主要な登場人物である豊臣秀吉。日本史上屈指の人気キャラクターだが、その彼が日本に入ったばかりの西洋音楽を聴いて、絶賛したのをご存知だろうか。

1591 年 3 月。聚楽第。 20 歳をちょっと過ぎたばかりの４人の青年が、太閤秀吉の前でヨーロッパの楽器を奏でた。演奏された楽器は、クラヴォ（小型の鍵盤楽器）、小型のハープ、リュート、ラベキーニャ（小型のヴァイオリンのような弦楽器）。秀吉は彼らの演奏を大変気に入り、３度にわたってアンコールを所望したという。

青年たちは、九州のキリシタン大名たちの名代としてヨーロッパに派遣された日本初の公的な外国訪問団「天正遣欧少年使節」のメンバーである。実際に演奏された曲は不明だが、音楽史家の故皆川達夫氏は、ルネッサンス音楽の大家ジョスカン・デプレの名曲で、ヨーロッパで大人気だったシャンソン「千々の悲しみ」を候補曲として挙げている。

実際、青年たちの腕前は確かだったらしい。出発前には日本の神学校で楽器を学び、旅の間も寄港地で練習に励んだ。ポルトガルのエヴォラの街では、使節の２人が大司教の要望に応じて大聖堂のオルガンで見事な腕前を披露し、一同の喝采を受けたという。

「天正遣欧少年使節」もまた、前回この連載で触れた「対抗宗教改革」の賜物である。プロテスタントの攻勢に対抗するべく世界への布教に乗り出したカトリック勢力が、日本におけるさらなる布教に対する援助を目的に、キリシタン大名とつながりがあり（実際は必ずしもそうではなかったが）模範的な日本の少年信者をヨーロッパへ派遣したのが「天正少年遣欧使節」だ。さまざまな困難に遭遇しながらヨーロッパに到着した一行は、行く先々で大歓迎を受けた。それはカトリック教会にとっては自分たちが地の果てまで浸透した証であり、日本にとってはその存在が証明された出来事となった。

フェリペ２世に謁見した少年使節

少年たちの最終目的地はもちろんヴァチカンだったが、ヴァチカン訪問の前年、 1584 年に、彼らはヨーロッパ一の権力者の謁見にあずかっている。スペイン国王、フェリペ２世である。

ハプスブルク家が 16 世紀に「太陽の沈むことがない（常に領土のどこかで太陽が輝いている）」大帝国へと発展したのは、第３回でご紹介したマクシミリアン 1 世の子供たちがスペイン王家と縁組したからである。マクシミリアンの孫カール５世（神聖ローマ皇帝）はスペイン王カルロス１世を兼ね、その子の代でハプスブルク家はスペイン系とオーストリア系に分かれたが、スペイン国王となったフェリペ２世は在位中にポルトガルを併合、また新大陸やアジアに植民地を獲得して大帝国の盟主となった。

歴史的には「悪役」のイメージ

だが歴史上の位置付けでは、フェリペ２世は悪役である。フェリペはオーストリアのハプスブルク家以上に、「対抗宗教改革」のリーダーとして権勢を振るった。「異端者が入り込むくらいなら領土を失い、１００回死んだ方がまし」とまで発言し、プロテスタントにとどまらずユダヤ教やイスラム教からの改宗者にも目を光らせ、少しでも疑わしければ捕らえて拷問にかけ、時には処刑した。「異端者火刑」は大いなる見せ物でもあった。その様子はヴェルディのオペラ《ドン・カルロス》で垣間見ることができる。

近年、フェリペ治下での異端審問が従来言われていたほど厳しくなかったという研究が出てきたが、彼の弾圧に反発して、オランダが独立戦争に突入したのは史実である。その結果フェリペは、マクシミリアン以来帝国の一部だった、最も富裕な領土を失ったのだった。

日本における布教を牽引したイエズス会もスペインの組織であり、少年使節がフェリペを表敬訪問するのは当然だった。宮殿と礼拝堂を兼ねた大建築であるエル・エスコリアル宮殿で彼らに謁見したフェリペは喜び、少年たちと一緒にミサに参列している。フェリペの宮廷には立派な宮廷楽団があり、信心深い国王のため、壮麗な典礼音楽が演奏されていた。少年たちが聴いたのは、当代を代表する宗教音楽の大家、トマス・ルイス・デ・ビクトリアの音楽だったかもしれない。

スペイン王室でも音楽を重要視

オーストリア・ハプスブルク家同様、スペイン・ハプスブルク家の音楽組織もインターナショナルだった。フェリペの父カールは、ニコラ・ゴンベールをはじめとするフランドルの有名な音楽家をスペインに連れてきた。フェリペの母ファナの一族であるスペイン宮廷でも音楽は盛んで、ラテン語の教会音楽に加え、スペイン語の歌も歌われていた。カールの代に二つの楽団は合併し、帝国の富を背景に、ヨーロッパ随一の王室礼拝堂楽団が出来上がった。ちなみに皆川氏が秀吉の御前演奏の曲の候補として挙げている「千々の悲しみ」は、カール５世が愛好し、「皇帝の歌」と呼ばれた曲である。

フェリペ自身もヴィエラという楽器を弾くなど多少音楽は嗜んだが、夢中になるというほどではなかったようだ。それよりも音楽は、日々のミサや年中行事を通じて、やはり王室の権威を表すプロパガンダとして用いられた。カールとフェリペの２代に仕えた有名な音楽家に、盲目のオルガニスト、アントニオ・デ・カベソンがいるが、フェリペはフランドルのオルガン製作者ジル・ブレヴォスに、エル・エスコリアルの礼拝堂に大オルガンを建造させている。天正少年使節もまた、巨大な大聖堂を満たす華麗な音響に震え上がったのではないだろうか。

美術にも情熱を傾けたフェリペ２世

美術もまたフェリペの情熱の対象だった。エル・エスコリアルの絵画コレクションは、イタリア・ルネッサンスの大家ティツィアーノから、奇想天外な画風で知られるヒエロニムス・ボス、専属の肖像画家だったコエーリョまで、ルネッサンスを一望できる大コレクションである。エル・グレコもこの時代に活躍しているが、グレコの個性的な作風はフェリペの好みではなかったようだ。

ヴェルディの名作オペラのモチーフにも

滅多に笑わなかったという堅物のフェリペだが、コレクションには官能的な神話画も少なくない。ティツィアーノの『エウロペの略奪』は、大神ゼウスがフェニキアの王女エウロペを略奪し、多くの子供を成したというギリシャ神話のエピソードにちなんだもので、エウロペは豊穣のシンボルであり、この絵はフェリペの３度目の結婚にあたって贈られたものである。

妃はフランス王女エリザベート（スペイン語読みイサベル）で、前述のオペラ《ドン・カルロス》のヒロインでもある。オペラでは夫婦仲は冷えているが、実際の夫婦仲は悪くなく、フェリペは 18 歳年下のエリザベートを可愛がり、２人の娘にも恵まれた。ただエリザベートは体が弱く、 23 歳の若さで産褥で亡くなってしまった。この出来事と、その直前に起こった長男のドン・カルロスの獄死という悲劇が、フェリペに批判的なプロテスタントだったドイツの劇作家フリードリヒ・シラーによって、エリザベートがドン・カルロスと愛し合っていたという荒唐無稽なストーリーになり、ヴェルディのオペラにもなってしまったのだった。

ベラスケスを重用、政治にも参画

スペイン王家の芸術好きは受け継がれる。２世の孫フェリペ４世はベラスケスを保護し、宮廷画家に加えて官僚のトップまで任せたが、他にもルーベンス、スルバランといった大家たちを後援している。ベラスケスの筆で繰り返し描かれたのが、前回ご紹介した４世の娘で、レオポルト１世の最初の妃マルガリータだ。

フェリペ４世は厳格な祖父とは違い、音楽付きの劇を好んだ。そしてこの時代、芸術にはイタリアからの風が吹いた。在世中、マドリードに建造したブエン・レティーロ宮殿には宮廷劇場があり、イタリア人の美術家が舞台装置を担当。イタリア・オペラで大人気だったカストラートも４世の宮廷で活動している。ベラスケスの作品も、傑作『ラス・メニーナス』をはじめ極めて演劇的だ。

４世の時代には、スペインのミュージカルである「サルスエラ」も生まれている。狩の館である「パラシオ・デ・サルスエラ」で、セリフで進行する音楽劇が上演されるようになり、これが後の「サルスエラ」へと発展したのだった。

スペイン宮廷で活躍した音楽家の中で、最も名前が知られている人物が活躍したのはフェリペ５世の時代である。だがこの時、スペインはもうハプスブルク家の時代ではなかった。繰り返された近親婚の悪影響でフェリペ４世の子カルロス２世には子供ができず、家督はカルロス２世の遺言により、母方のフランス、ブルボン朝のフェリペ５世に譲られる。オーストリアのハプスブルク家が黙っているはずもなく、スペイン継承戦争が起こるが、結局フランスが勝利。スペインはブルボン朝になった。そして宮廷ではイタリアの音楽が開花する。フェリペ５世の２人目の妃でイタリア、パルマ公国の公女エリザベッタ・ファルネーゼは、イタリアから音楽家を大量に連れてきて、ヨーロッパを席巻していたイタリア・オペラがスペイン宮廷をも魅了することになったのだった。

オペラの歌声は、なんと王のうつ病にも絶大な効果を発揮する。王妃は 1737 年、当代一と讃えられたカストラート（去勢歌手）のファリネッリを宮廷に招く。フェリペ５世はその美声の虜になり、宮廷でも最高級の年俸を約束して王室付きの歌手に雇い入れた。ファリネッリは毎晩、王の就寝前にたった４曲歌うだけで病を癒やし、贅沢三昧の暮らしを手に入れたのである。

動画はファリネッリが主人公の映画「カストラート」より カストラートの声は、ソプラノとカウンターテナーの声を合わせて合成されている

そしてもう一人、この王朝を飾った名音楽家を見逃してはならない。

ドメニコ・スカルラッティ（ 1685-1757 ）。ナポリを本拠に大活躍したアレッサンドロ・スカルラッティの息子で、チェンバロの名手である。ポルトガル王女マリア・バルバラの音楽教師になり、王女がスペイン王太子のフェルナンドと結婚したのに伴ってマドリードの宮廷にやってきた。本当はオペラから宗教音楽までなんでも書けたのだが、職務のおかげで膨大な数の、そしてリズムや音色にスペイン色がこだます斬新なチェンバロ・ソナタを書き、それで歴史に名を残した。

大聖堂に轟くミサから華麗なオペラ、そして宮殿の私室でのチェンバロ・ソナタまで。スペイン宮廷の音楽もまた、ハプスブルク家を通じて破格の豊かさを獲得したのだった。（音楽評論家・加藤浩子）

article_text:
“Night Feeds,” a psychological horror short from Rana Roy starring May Calamawy (“ Moon Knight ”), will open the first edition of the Yami International Film Festival , Tokyo’s new showcase for horror and darker genre fare.

“Breeder,” from Alex Goyette, will close the festival, which runs Nov. 20–26 at Human Trust Cinema Shibuya.

The event is run by Yami Inc., a Japanese company known for horror exhibitions and other genre-themed attractions. Its goal is to introduce Japanese audiences to new horror filmmakers from home and abroad. An open call ran from late May to the end of August and brought in 182 entries from 40 countries and territories. Six features were picked for the feature competition and eight shorts for the short competition.

Related Stories

Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’

Yami chose to open with a short and close with a feature. The organizers believe both formats will shape where the genre goes next.

Popular on Variety

“Night Feeds” was made at the American Film Institute. It follows a new mother whose isolation and anxiety become tangled up with dread about a war in the world outside, until it’s hard to tell what’s real and what’s a nightmare. Calamawy’s credits also include Lee Cronin’s “The Mummy.”

“Breeder” is a horror thriller that mixes dark comedy with scares in a story built around breeding. Dot-Marie Jones, a multiple Emmy nominee for “Glee,” plays Patti, a character pushed close to madness.

Roy and Goyette will both travel to Tokyo to sit on the jury. Japanese actress Sukezane Kiki, whose international credits include “Heroes Reborn,” “Lost in Space” and “Westworld,” completes the three-person panel.

The feature competition includes two Asian premieres: Zoe Berriatúa’s Spanish title “Buffet Libre” and Abner Pastoll’s South Korea-U.K. co-production “Nervous.” The other four features will have their Japan premieres. On the shorts side, Rick Kawanaka’s Japanese entry “The Pot” will be the festival’s only world premiere. Katagiri Eriko’s “When You Open the Door” will screen as a special presentation.

Producer Wada Arihiro (“Silver Express,” “Fujiko”) is the festival director and also heads programming.

“Physical terror, psychological horror, the unease lurking beneath the everyday, and dark humor. The films presented at Yami each explore ‘fear’ in their own distinctive ways,” Wada said. “Rather than simply fitting within the boundaries of established genres, we sought out films that unsettle the senses, challenge expectations, and reveal new forms of fear. Come to Shibuya, Tokyo, and experience the cutting edge of horror from around the world.”

The lineup:

Feature Competition “Species,” Marion Le Corroller (France, Belgium) “Buffet Libre,” Zoe Berriatúa (Spain) “Hold to Death: Hand in Hand,” Alex Wang (Taiwan) “Gaua,” Paul Urkijo Alijo (Spain, U.S.) “Nervous,” Abner Pastoll (South Korea, U.K.) “No Rest for the Wicked,” Kasper Kalle (Denmark, Iceland)

Short Competition “Idols,” Matt Halsall (South Korea, Japan, U.K.) “The Pot,” Rick Kawanaka (Japan) “Dormant,” Cris Gavrilova (Russia) “Bestiary,” Anne Zinn-Justin (France) “Amira,” Javier Yañez Sanz (Spain) “Hollow Paths,” Francesco Madeo (Italy) “Floor,” Jo Bareun (South Korea) “Happy,” Victor Basallote (Spain)

Opening Film “Night Feeds,” Rana Roy (U.S.)

Closing Film “Breeder,” Alex Goyette (U.S., Canada)

Special Screening “When You Open the Door,” Katagiri Eriko (Japan)

Rich Felgate, Olive Nwosu, Gwendoline Christie, Jessie Buckley, Imran Perretta, Rachel Taparjan

The filmmakers behind We, The Hated, Lady , Ish and Something Familiar are the four winners of the 2026 BFI and Chanel Filmmaker Awards.

Now in their fifth year, the awards aim to champion creativity, culture and craftsmanship and support future British creative talents, with each recipient receiving £20,000.

The winners were unveiled by new jury members Jessie Buckley and Gwendoline Christie alongside existing jurors Edward Enninful, Marie-Louise Khondji and BFI CEO Ben Roberts at an event held today at London’s Claridges Hotel (October 14).

The jury described Rich Felgate’s We, The Hated, which opened Sheffield Doc Fest earlier this year and follows UK climate protest movement Just Stop Oil, as “urgent and brave, powerfully conveying the impact on the individuals as well as raising pressing questions about the wider political context”.

Olive Nwosu’s Nigeria-set feature debut Lady premiered in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival where it won the special jury award for an acting ensemble and also screened in Berlin’s Panorama section. The jury described it as a “big cinematic movie, immediately transporting us to Lagos, demonstrating ambition and craft rare for a directorial debut”.

Imran Perretta’s feature debut Ish had its world premiere in the Critics’ Week section at Venice in 2025, winning the audience award, before going on to play at the London Film Festival last year. The jury described the film, which Perretta co-wrote with Enda Walsh and draws on his own experiences of racial profiling growing up, as a “wonderful and deeply moving film, overwhelming the cinema screen with an authentic and emotionally true story that is both incredibly intimate but also universal”.

Meanwhile, the jury praised Rachel Taparjan’s “bravery and total openness”, describing Something Familiar as a “naked, unself-conscious revelation of self”. The documentary, which follows Taparjan as she returns to her native Romania having been adopted and brought to England as a child, world premiered at CPH: DOX and won the Chicken and Egg Vision Award at Cannes docs in progress in 2025.

Previous winners of the awards include Harry Lighton in 2025 for Pillion, Kathryn Ferguson in 2022 with Sinead O’Connor documentary Nothing Compares, Savannah Leaf in 2023 with Earth Mama and director and producer Pinny Grylls in 2024 with Grand Theft Hamlet.

Bifa breakthrough performance longlist includes ‘Extra Geography’, ‘Effi o Blaenau’ actors

article_text:
The lingering trauma shared by two middle-class families, once friendly but now estranged following a tragic camping incident, is finally addressed through the unlikely prism of a high-school drama club production in “ Between Us ,” Shingo Matsumura ’s well-intentioned, yet only fitfully successful, exploration of unprocessed grief. The writer-director’s fourth feature film premieres as part of the Tokyo Film Festival ’s revamped and newly competitive Nippon Cinema Now section and is bolstered by a quartet of assured performances from its female leads.

Related Stories

'To Be Ordinary' Review: A Compassionate, Even-Handed Taiwanese Family Melodrama

‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Review: China’s Oscar Entry Is a Breakneck Blockbuster That Mixes Food Porn With Wartime Devastation

Ririka Kawashima is most impressive as the shellshocked teenager Makoto in a story that sees mothers and daughters emerge from the emotional fallout of losing a loved one to shoulder the burden of recovery and reconciliation. Never lacking in ambition, yet left somewhat wanting in execution, commercial prospects for “Between Us” may well be limited to specialist showcases with a particular focus on nurturing emerging voices still honing their craft.

In a brief yet crucial prologue, 10-year-old Kasumi and her parents set out on a countryside camping trip. They were set to be joined by Kasumi’s classmate Makoto and her family, but she is sick and her father is called into the office unexpectedly. As a result, only Makoto’s eight-year-old brother Kenji goes with the other family, and upon arrival at the campsite, scampers around excitedly with a butterfly net, while being warned not to wander too far.

Six years later, and the domestic landscape has changed dramatically for both households. High-schooler Makoto (Kawashima) lives with her mother, Emi (Akiko Kikuchi) — who is now an emotional wreck — while her father (Yoichiro Saito) has moved out, lost his office job, and now scrapes together a living as a delivery driver. Makoto bristles when an elderly neighbor casually mentions her brother, while Emi becomes all but catatonic when a colleague at the library where she works asks after her “little one.”

Kasumi (Anna Kurasawa) and her family appear to be faring somewhat better. They are still together and have added a now five-year-old daughter, Chika, to their brood. But when mother Fumiko (Asami Usuda) comments that their youngest was complaining about never seeing her father (Takahiro Miura) smile, the cracks beneath this veneer of domestic bliss quickly become apparent.

These early sequences display a keen ability from Matsumura to paint a tragic picture of malignant, festering grief from a past tragedy, without the need for any overt explanation. However, in a frustrating and unnecessary misstep, an out-of-place news report on a car radio confirms that Kenji disappeared on a camping trip with family friends six years earlier, and that the police have not ruled out the possibility of foul play. Not only does this heavy-handed over-clarification — beyond earshot of any character and included solely for the benefit of the audience — erase any sense of mystery surrounding what has happened, but it also suggests a forthcoming procedural element to the narrative that never materializes.

Instead, the film turns its attention to Makoto and Kasumi, who find themselves not only attending the same high school, but enrolled as sole members of the school’s struggling drama club. Simultaneously, Fumiko and Emi cross paths at the library, where the revelation that the family at least tangentially responsible for her son’s death now have an adorable little sprog of their own, threatens to send Emi into an emotional tailspin.

While both patriarchs prove utterly ineffectual in processing what has happened, and their wives reluctant to engage, it falls to the younger generation to acknowledge the suffocating sense of loss that has smothered and crippled both families. Makoto and Kasumi resolve to produce a play dramatizing precisely this decision to reconcile, leaning into the residual affection they still hold for each other and, unlike their parents, a desire to process the hostility that has manifested in the hope of letting go and moving forward.

As it crawls timidly towards its climactic performance, “Between Us” frustrates as frequently as it impresses, teasing at promises of meta-textual experimentation or cathartic revelations, precious few of which come to fruition. In many ways, Matsumura’s film recalls Lee Jong-un’s 2019 Korean drama “Birthday,” which observed the paralyzing impact of the 2014 Sewol ferry disaster, in which more than 300 people died, without ever reenacting the event itself.

The director’s resolve to leave crucial questions unanswered is bold and praiseworthy, but he might have gone further still. Similarly, his stance that his teenage heroines are more willing and better equipped emotionally to forgive, heal and reconcile than their parents might have benefited from a modicum of conflict or pushback from the older generation. Nevertheless, despite these shortcomings, “Between Us” remains a tidily assembled little package that brandishes a welcome glimmer of dramatic ambition, and at the very least, provides its female cast with a stage on which to shine.

article_text:
A bold juxtaposition of real and unreal worlds is at the heart of Guillermo del Toro’s visually inventive fantasy about Franco-ite Spain. It’s so audacious and so technically accomplished, and arrives here garlanded with so many radiant superlatives, that I wish I liked it more. The film’s political dimension is never quite as lavishly or as enthusiastically achieved as its fantasy life, however, and its energies are asymmetric: the surface world of history is clogged compared to the sheer energy of its subterranean dreamscape.

Like Del Toro’s 2001 picture The Devil’s Backbone, Pan’s Labyrinth is about the Spanish civil war. It is 1944; the struggle against the Republicans has been won in Spain. D-Day, and Hitler’s imminent collapse in Europe, are distant and unwelcome rumours. A fierce Franco-ite Captain Vidal, played by the incomparably sinister Sergi López, prepares to welcome his pregnant bride to the family home in the forest, which he is reinforcing as a military redoubt because it is surrounded by Republican guerrillas holding out in the woods. His new wife Carmen (Adriana Gil) is a widow who has accepted Vidal’s proposal of marriage out of loneliness; Ofélia (Ivana Baquero), her daughter by her first marriage, is terrified of this wicked stepfather, as well she might be. On the very first night, Vidal brutally beats and murders two suspected Republicans - a horribly violent scene - putting his bad-guy status beyond doubt.

Ofélia has somewhere to escape. This intelligent, bookish child has discovered a secret labyrinth beneath the house inhabited by a magnificent, awe-inspiring faun who hails Ofélia as a Princess, but tells her she must carry out terrifying tasks to enter into her destiny; this she does, without telling the grown-ups of this strange other world beneath their feet. Nor is Ofélia the only double agent in the film. Vidal’s housekeeper and doctor have treacherous Republican sympathies.

Fascism is perhaps the ultimate example of that sleep of reason which brings forth monsters. Del Toro’s monsters are pretty extraordinary. He has said that his designs are influenced by Arthur Rackham, the English Victorian artist who illustrated Lewis Carroll and Shakespeare. This description doesn’t do justice to the originality of Del Toro’s pictorial devices. At the film’s beginning, Ofélia has a little pinafore dress recalling Alice; her name echoes Hamlet’s love, but her self-reliance and grit far surpass that passive Shakespearian figure. Maybe her name is a female variant of Orpheus.

At any rate, it is an excellent performance from 12-year-old Baquero. Ofélia must confront a giant and loathsome toad in a claustrophobic tunnel. She must square up to the giant and imperious faun, Pan. Most dauntingly of all, she has to approach the nightmarish figure of the Pale Man, whose eyes are in his hands - he is able to see her when he holds his palms up to the sides of his head. That extraordinary image alone is worth the price of admission.

What do these creatures say about fascism? Or, what does fascism say about them? Del Toro asks us to consider Pan’s exotic world side-by-side with political history. We have to consume them on equal terms, like chewing cake and cheese together. It’s a bold and intriguing proposition, but I’m not sure it comes off. Del Toro does well to remind us of the cruel reality of Franco’s Spain: a fascist state tacitly encouraged by many as a bulwark against communism, and seen by many more as an example of the historical inevitability of extreme nationalism. These are the bad guys who were not defeated, and perhaps Del Toro’s fantasy of the ambiguous, tyrannical faun is not merely a dramatising of Ofélia’s private anxieties, but a way of working through Spain’s collective fear and distrust of its own past. Either way, I felt the movie was a series of four or five brilliant images, like illustrative plates from a Victorian volume, or frames from a graphic novel. There was no overwhelming narrative drive or inner dramatic life to animate them. But what amazing pictures Del Toro dreams up.

title_original: Libraryman : François Halard : Conversation with Claude
editorial_title_zh: Libraryman : François Halard : Conversation with Claude
editorial_excerpt_zh: 摄影是一种语言吗？人们可能会这么认为，因为任何人都可以通过它来表达自己。然而，图像并不会说话，尽管它也并非全然哑口无言。它让我们看到（并因此去思考）某些事物。它诉说着什么，但其语言是经过编码的，要想破译它，就必须关注构成它的各个元素。一旦观察者超越了被动的观看，交流就变得大有可能。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影是一种语言吗？人们可能会这么认为，因为任何人都可以通过它来表达自己。然而，图像并不会说话，尽管它也并非全然哑口无言。它让我们看到（并因此去思考）某些事物。它诉说着什么，但其语言是经过编码的，要想破译它，就必须关注构成它的各个元素。一旦观察者超越了被动的观看，交流就变得大有可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影展露出自身，观者的感知力则可以通过其中的光线、对比度、色彩的和谐、黑白的细微差别、取景中对某些元素赋予或轻或重的权重……或者定格瞬间所选择的那个时机，投影于其中。所有这些符号都至关重要，并赋予意义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由此，一场无声的对话悄然展开：观者通过展出的符号来解读艺术家的技术与美学选择，讨论的空间也随之浮现。这场对话似乎成为了艺术家意图与观者解读所得之接受度之间的交汇点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在拍摄莫奈位于吉维尼的花园时，弗朗索瓦·阿拉尔（François Halard）并不满足于带回一系列宝丽来照片。他着手在原始快照的放大版上添抹颜料，或是细腻的斑驳笔触，或是呈滴落状，仿佛要从影像表面渗出。既然宝丽来本身就带有偶然性甚至印象派的清晰度，那么经过涂绘的第二阶段，便似乎赋予了这种目光交流以物质形态。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在精美的书籍《Conversation with Claude》中，或者在巴黎摄影展（Paris Photo）的 Ruttkowski;68 画廊展位上，当我们看到这些混合媒介作品时，阿拉尔并非试图记录他的驻留；正如克劳德·莫奈一样，他也展现了自己对风景沉思的独特视角。为该书撰写导言的歌剧导演文森特·于盖（Vincent Huguet）告诉我们：“每一笔都像是一片花瓣，有时带有印象派的轻盈，有时带有表现主义的能量，顺便让人想起，这座睡莲池也是美国抽象绘画的熔炉之一。我们既身处日本庭园又身处纽约，既在诺曼底又在阿尔勒的工作室中。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一个多世纪后，弗朗索瓦·阿拉尔将自己置于诠释光线、水波和植被的位置，通过具象与抽象相结合的技术，玩味着倒影与虚焦，从而呈献了他与印象派之间独特而亲密的对话。摄影及其现实与绘画的敏感符号交织在一起，将那些最初泼洒颜料的人与唤醒其记忆的当代目光之间积极交流的理念化为具象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "让-雅克·阿德尔（Jean-Jacques Ader）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Conversation with Claude》，作者弗朗索瓦·阿拉尔，由托尼·塞德泰格/Libraryman（Tony Cederteg/Libraryman）于11月1日出版。https://libraryman.se/。这些作品将在 Ruttkowski;68 画廊于 2026 年巴黎摄影展（Paris Photo）期间举办的个展中展出。信息：https://www.ruttkowski68.com/exhibition/conversation-with-claude/", "links": [{"text": "https://libraryman.se/", "url": "https://libraryman.se/"}, {"text": "https://www.ruttkowski68.com/exhibition/conversation-with-claude/", "url": "https://www.ruttkowski68.com/exhibition/conversation-with-claude/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
Is photography a language? One might think so, since anyone can express themselves through it. Yet an image does not speak, though it is not mute either. It gives us something to see (and therefore to think about). It says things, but its language is coded, and to decipher it one must pay attention to the elements that make it up. Once the observer has moved beyond passive viewing, an exchange becomes far more likely.

Photography reveals itself, and the sensibility of the beholder can project itself into it through the light present, its contrasts, the harmony of colors, the nuances of black and white, the importance given in the framing to certain elements or not… or the instant chosen to freeze the moment. All of these signs matter and give meaning.

Thus a silent dialogue takes hold: the artist’s technical and aesthetic choices can be interpreted by the viewer through the signs on display, and a space for discussion can emerge. This conversation seems to be a meeting point between an artist’s intention and its reception as interpreted by a viewer.

In photographing Monet’s gardens at Giverny, François Halard was not content to bring back a series of Polaroids. He set about adding paint to enlargements of the original snapshots, either in delicate, speckled touches or in a dripping manner, which seem to ooze from the surface of the images. Since Polaroids already have a chance-driven, even impressionistic, definition, the second, painted stage seems to give material form to this exchange of gazes.

In revealing these hybrid works to us in the beautiful book “ Conversation with Claude ,” or on the stand of the Ruttkowski;68 gallery at Paris Photo, Halard was not trying to document his stay; he too, just like Claude Monet, offers a personal version of his contemplation of the landscape. Opera director Vincent Huguet, who wrote the introductory essay to the book, tells us: “ Each touch resembles the petal of a flower, at times with an impressionist lightness, at times with an expressionist energy recalling, in passing, that the lily pond was also one of the crucibles of American abstract painting. We find ourselves at once in a Japanese garden and in New York, in Normandy and in a studio in Arles. ”

More than a century later, François Halard has put himself in the position of interpreting the light, the waters and the vegetation, and, through a figurative-abstract technique, of playing with reflections and blurs, to deliver his singular and intimate conversation with Impressionism. Photography and its reality blend with the sensitive signs of painting, giving concrete form to the idea of an active exchange between the one who first drew the splashes and the contemporary eye that revives its memory.

Jean-Jacques Ader

“Conversation with Claude” by François Halard, published November 1 by Tony Cederteg/Libraryman. https://libraryman.se/ . The works will be presented in a solo show by the Ruttkowski;68 gallery on the occasion of Paris Photo 2026. Info: https://www.ruttkowski68.com/exhibition/conversation-with-claude/

"你在挂置这件作品时，以非常有趣的方式运用了布展设计；能跟我们聊聊你在挂画风格上做出的一些决定吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这座城市已经变了。我认为这些年来我受到安保人员和执法人员骚扰的部分原因，是因为城市的那片区域情况变得非常糟糕。由于种种糟糕状况，这座城市也受到了许多负面宣传。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在上次大选期间，我思考了“从此幸福快乐”这个问题。这个问题直指傲慢与否认、公民正在经历的虐待，以及掌权者漠不关心的普遍态度。", "在我决定留在德班并在那里创作后，首先吸引我的是光线。德班的光线不可思议，清透干脆。它感觉像是一张白纸。我们有彼得·麦肯齐（Peter McKenzie）等许多拍摄过德班的摄影师，所以我不是第一个，但作为长期在约翰内斯堡生活和工作、并多次因家庭原因造访德班的人，直到我去度蜜月度假之前，我从未见过那种美丽的光线。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "找到公寓后，我开始跑步并做有氧运动。每天早晨我都沿着海滩跑步。有一群年轻人——那是2021年，在两次封城之间——他们每天早上聚在一起锻炼。我会慢跑回来，看到这些年轻人，我非常喜欢这种氛围。人们当时正试图寻找应对那个时期创伤的方法。这也是一种觉察，关乎照顾好自己的身体和健康。一天早晨，我决定过去跟他们打招呼，问怎么加入这个班。我被告知他们所做的一部分内容是专注于减重，我可以免费加入这些课程；我通过购买产品来支持他们的业务。就这样，我认识了一位教练，并会向他们订购茶之类的产品。我就是这样找到了我的第一个社群，并通过他们融入了这座城市。其中一些人直到现在仍然是我的朋友，尽管那支健身队伍已经不复存在了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artthrob.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/North-Beach-meeting-of-strangers-2023-640x387.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtThrob", Courtesy of KZNSA Gallery.", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "还有另一群人是来过圣诞假期的。我从未真正想过水的暴力性，水是多么具有暴力性。他们中的一群人在游泳时遇到了麻烦。幸运的是，救生员就在附近，能够跳进水里迅速救出他们。他们上来时，我已经在那儿了，我只拍了几张照片，但我其实对拍摄那一刻并不是很感兴趣。是在那之后，当他们被从海里救出、正往下走的时候，他们的脸上带着一种劫后余生的难以置信。我在这个令人震惊的时刻陪伴着他们四处走动，正是在那时，我决定为他们拍照。展览中有三张这样的照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "说到暴力，这次展览也呈现了七月骚乱的暴力，以及洪水的暴力。这件作品正在对“从此幸福快乐”提出质疑。曾有一位学生问我我的作品是否具有政治性，因为她读了照片的标题，觉得这件作品不仅仅关于婚礼和蜜月。确实如此。即使在作品中我审视与水的关系的那部分，也存在这样一个问题：在一个从未有时间去正视、去谈论疗愈的国家里，这种关系意味着什么。我曾见证人们将大海视为一个疗愈的空间，而不仅仅是休闲和享乐。有些人去那里抛开过去；这是一个净化的场所。作品中就有这样的人物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artthrob.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Gallery-Views-2026-10-Exhibition-Sabelo-Mlangeni-Honeymoon.-The-happily-ever-after_-13-scaled-1-640x427.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtThrob", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Installation View: Honeymoon. Courtesy of KZNSA Gallery.", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个系列可能与以往的作品略有不同，它包含了风格上的变化——我们在不同尺寸的彩色黑白照片中看到了建筑图像、身体碎片、人物、场地等。你能谈谈你为这个系列选择这种创作方式的考量吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当你谈论城市时，它大多是黑白的，但在作品中，我们看到了这些不同的形式、身体和建筑共存。我不会说这是我的作品中第一次出现这种情况，但这里我确实加入了彩色照片。色彩也与寻找过期胶卷有关；我一直在收集过期胶卷，因为我对某种特定的色彩感兴趣，也对使用旧胶卷的意义感兴趣。使用过期胶卷会产生一点色彩偏移，我对这一点很感兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这也是我第一次创作出色彩感觉与黑白摄影别无二致的彩色照片。我一直在使用彩色胶片并进行练习，但我发现自己在相机里装入彩色胶片和黑白胶片时的思考方式是不一样的。那是两种不同的思维方式。因此，这也是我第一次将我的眼睛如何看待色彩呈现出来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如我之前所解释的，随着时间的推移，一个空间会对你产生某种影响或触动，我认为这在作品中得到了体现。由于我的生活和工作穿梭于约翰内斯堡和德班之间，我提到了这里的光线：德班的光线清澈明朗，正如这座城市的灵魂与活力一样。它平静而放松。这与约翰内斯堡不同，那是一座奋斗者的城市，每个人都在奔忙，能量也截然不同。那里的灵魂带有一点灰暗。这些感受和情绪会流露出来，并通过作品的呈现方式得到增强。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artthrob.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sabelo-Mlangeni-Six-months-after-the-flood-Mvuzane-Clermont-2022-640x644.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtThrob", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "萨贝洛·姆兰盖尼（Sabelo Mlangeni），《洪水过后六个月，姆武扎内·克莱蒙特》（Six months after the flood, Mvuzane Clermont），（2022年）。图片由 KZNSA 美术馆提供。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
A feature by ArtThrob Editors on the 29th of October 2026. This should take you 9 minutes to read.

KZNSA Gallery 04.10 - 02.11.2026

Sabelo Mlangeni’s ‘Honeymoon. The happily ever after?’ is a body of work built over five years, inspired by a honeymoon trip to eThekwini (Durban). The work is an intimate account of multifaceted life in Durban, capturing the everyday experiences of beachgoers and passersby alongside architectural frames that highlight a sense of instability and the energy of the city. Framed as a question, the work explores the city’s history and contentious present, reflecting on structural effects: a failing government, environmental impact such as the 2022 floods and infrastructural collapse. While looking at the city with a sense of clarity and fresh eyes, Mlangeni also considers its parallels of beauty and decay, joy and struggle, and emerges with quiet moments of humanity.

We interviewed Mlangeni on the work, following its presentation at the KZNSA Gallery (4 Oct – 2 Nov 2026).

Sabelo Mlangeni, I love you Durban, (2023). Courtesy of KZNSA Gallery.

The work was very well received when you showed it in Cape Town in 2025. How does it feel to be showing this work in the very same town where it was developed?

It is totally different, but at the same time exciting to see the work in Durban. I’m especially thinking about the choice of the colours – the orange, for me, is more of the sunrise in the city, and the blue is the distance of water. Sunrise and sunset, settled water.

Presenting the work in Durban suddenly makes sense.

Even though I had a few unpleasant incidents at the beginning when I was installing the show, which really affected me, the work did go on. Somehow I had to split myself into two. I had to focus on what was happening, but at the same time I had to make sure that the show was realised and was a successful show.

How is it received? Durban is totally different from cities like Johannesburg and Cape Town. The scene is very small. But my appreciation is mostly of how photographers are receiving this show and appreciating having a show that focuses on photography, which is something very rare.

It’s my first solo show in Durban, and although for five years I’ve been going back and forth between Johannesburg and Durban, it’s not a city where I can truly say I have a big audience. So I wouldn’t, at this point, say exactly how the show is received. Since the show opened, I’ve spent time with students from photography and fine art, and also the general public.

Installation View: Honeymoon. The happily ever after? Courtesy of KZNSA Gallery.

You play around with installation in a very interesting way to hang this work; can you tell us about some of the decisions you made in terms of your hanging style?

If you have noticed, in recent years I have been very interested in exhibition-making, and in thinking about different ways to read photographs, and to install or hang photographs: how photographs take up a space, a white wall. With each and every work, I find a language or a tone that I use to install or place the work in the space.

I think of the work Ngiyobona Phambili, for example. In terms of colours, I chose forest green because the work was mostly dealing with landscape, and there is also a certain way of framing that I used for that body of work. With Isivumelwano, which explored marriage ceremonies in Black communities- it was mostly white – just a straight line, a clean line, thinking about a ring belt, a ring shadow, something very clean.

This time around, I wanted to work with wallpaper for the first time. I’ve never worked with wallpaper. The starting point was to overlap the wallpapers. If you saw the show in Cape Town and now this one, there is a continuation of the overlapping of the wallpapers. I think every work has its character, and you want to bring that character out through how it is displayed or seen. So the decisions come out of understanding the work, but also out of being in the space over time. It is something that is revealed through that.

The work itself questions ideas of a “happy ending” – but it is also very specific to the site of Durban – I wonder how you reflect on the city today (and how it has changed) since the work was made? In particular, how do you see the seaside itself changing and whether it might tell us a broader narrative about the city?

I decided to stop making work in the first chapter of the series when I got arrested by law enforcement for making photographs. But I had these experiences right from the beginning, where I was told many times that I’m not needed, or that they don’t want me there. Still, I kept on going back over the years, until this time.

The city has changed. I think some of the reasons why I was harassed by security and law enforcement over the years are partly because things have been going very badly in that part of the city. The city has also been getting a lot of bad publicity because of how bad things are.

During our last elections, I thought about this question of ‘happily ever after’. The question speaks to arrogance and denial, the ill-treatment that citizens are experiencing and a general attitude that those in power do not care.

I don’t know what kind of leadership can turn things around in the city, and we can simply say things are not different from the previous leadership.

Your work has always been incredibly specific about the lives of the people that you wish to document. Can you tell us a little bit about some of the figures you chose to document for this series?

It’s a different approach, and I find this challenge fascinating: to find oneself in a new space that is a place of pleasure, of honeymoon, of happiness, a holiday destination. That’s how I came to Durban. I went there for a honeymoon, and although I have family in Claremont, I decided I was going to stay in a hotel in Durban for the first time. It ended up being a five-year project, and even now I go back and forth. I consider that I’m based between these two cities now, Durban and Johannesburg.

I’ve been in Johannesburg for more than 20 years, so I already have a community. In Cape Town, too, there’s the art community, which is intimate but feels bigger.

After I decided that I wanted to stay in Durban and work there, the first thing that caught me was the light. The light in Durban is incredible, crisp. It felt like a blank canvas. We have photographers like Peter McKenzie and many others who have photographed Durban, so I’m not the first, but as someone who has lived and worked in Johannesburg for a long time and visited Durban many times for family, I had never seen that kind of beautiful light until I went for my honeymoon holiday.

After finding the apartment, I started running, and I did aerobics. Every morning I ran along the beach. There was a group of young people, – this was 2021, between lockdowns – who came together every morning to exercise. I would jog and come back and see these young people, and I loved what was happening. People were trying to find ways to deal with the trauma of that time. It was also about awareness, about taking care of one’s body and health. One morning I decided to go and greet them and ask how to join the class. I was told that part of what they do is to focus on weight loss and that I could join the sessions for free; I supported their business by buying products. So just like that, I was introduced to a coach, and I would order products like tea from them. That’s how I found my first community, which introduced me to the city. Some of them are still my friends even now, although the workout team doesn’t exist anymore.

That was my entry into the city. And there are also people, for example, who sell hats and beads to tourists, and I got to know those people around the beach.

There is also something about this work that is reminiscent of weddings. You know the bride and the groom, but sometimes you don’t know the guests. It’s the same when you come into any ceremony or event, and especially when you are there for a holiday.

There is one photograph in the series of a guy with a child on his chest. Many people assume this is a father and a son, and they are always surprised when I tell them it’s not like that. These two people had just met. They both came to Durban for a holiday and were at the beach at the same time, in two different groups. The baby was crying, one of those cries where even the mother doesn’t know what to do, and where, even as a first-time parent, you feel embarrassed because you’re with a group of other people and the child is crying nonstop. This guy went to the mother and asked for the baby. He took the baby, and immediately after he took the baby, the baby stopped crying. Then he put the baby on his chest, and that’s how I made that photograph. So there are moments like that. Sometimes I’m in that space: you meet a group of people, and you stay with them for more than two hours, and things just unfold.

Sabelo Mlangeni, North Beach, meeting of strangers (2023). Courtesy of KZNSA Gallery.

There is also another group of people who were visiting for the Christmas holidays. I never really thought about the violence of water, how violent water is. A group of them were swimming, and they got into trouble. Luckily, the lifesavers were close by and were able to jump in and quickly save them. When they came out, I was already there, and I took just a few shots, but I wasn’t really interested in making photographs of that moment. It was afterwards, when they were walking down after being taken out of the sea, and there was this disbelief in their faces that they had almost lost their lives. I walked around with them in this shocking moment, and that’s when I decided I would make photographs of them. In the exhibition, there are three of those photographs.

Speaking about violence, the exhibition also presents the violence of the July unrest, and the violence of the floods. This work is questioning the happily ever after. One student asked me if my work is political, because she had read the titles of the photographs and felt that the work is more than just about weddings and honeymoons. And it is true. Even in the part of the work where I’m looking at the relationship with water, there is the question of what that relationship means in a country that has never had time to address, to talk about, healing. I have witnessed people take the sea as a space of healing, not just of leisure and pleasure. Some people go there to throw away their past; it’s a place of cleansing. There are characters like that in the work.

Installation View: Honeymoon. The happily ever after? Courtesy of KZNSA Gallery.

The series, perhaps a bit different from previous works, includes variations in terms of style – we find architectural images, fragments of bodies, figures, sites, etc., in black and white alongside colour across varying sizes. Can you reflect on your choices to work in this way for this series?

When you speak of cities, it’s mostly black and white, but in this work we find these different forms, bodies and architecture together. I wouldn’t say it’s the first time in my work, but I did add colour photographs here. The colour was also about finding expired films; I was collecting expired films because I was interested in a certain kind of colour, and in the meaning of using old film. You get a little bit of colour shift with expired film, and I was interested in that.

This is also the body of work where, for the first time, I made photographs in colour that feel the same as how I see black and white. I’ve been working in colour and practising, but I’ve noticed in myself that the thinking is not the same when there is colour film in my camera and when there is black and white. They are two different ways of thinking. So this was a way, for the first time, to put out there how my eye sees colour.

As I explained before, a space influences or affects you in a certain way over time, and I think that is reflected in the work. Because I live and work between Johannesburg and Durban, I mention the light: it is crisp and clear in Durban, the same as the soul and energy of that city. It is calm and relaxed. It’s different from Johannesburg, the city of hustlers, where everyone is moving, and the energy is different. The soul is a little bit greyish. Those feelings and emotions come out and can be enhanced by how the work is presented.

Sabelo-Mlangeni, Six months after the flood, Mvuzane Clermont, (2022). Courtesy of KZNSA Gallery.

article_text:
シンシナティ美術館が145年にわたり収集してきたコレクションを紹介する展覧会 「シンシナティ美術館展～アメリカに渡ったヨーロッパの至宝～」 が、2027年1月10日まで 上野の森美術館 で開催されている。

本展では、コロー、クールベ、セザンヌ、モネ、ルノワール、ファン・ゴッホ、ピカソ、モディリアーニ、シャガールらによる絵画作品をはじめ、ドガやジャコメッティなどの彫刻作品を含む計84点を紹介する。そのうち81点が初来日作品となる。

ここでは、編集部が気になった展覧会公式グッズをピックアップして紹介する。

あみぐるみキーハンガー

ミッフィーやフィンセント・ファン・ゴッホをあみぐるみにした多彩なキーハンガーが登場。ミッフィーのあみぐるみは、オランダ発のハンドメイド・トイブランド「JUST DUTCH」とのコラボ商品で、フィンセント・ファン・ゴッホ《ポプラ林の中の二人》に着想を得ている。ゴッホが描いたポプラの木々や、地面を彩る可憐な花々を表現したアート衣装を身にまとっていてキュート。ミッフィーだけでなく、メラニーやボリスなど仲間たちも登場し、5種類の豊富なラインアップだ。各4180円（税込）。

ゴッホ自身をモチーフにした2種類のあみぐるみキーハンガーも登場。どちらもゴッホのトレードマークである麦わら帽子にふさふさの赤髭が印象的だ。「CROCHET KEYRING VINCENT2」（税込2860円）には洋服の胸元にひまわりのワンポイントが、「CROCHET KEYRING VINCENT3」（税込3300円）には小さなひまわりのチャームがついている。

ロルバーン ポケット付きメモL

ロルバーンのノートはクロード・モネ《ベリールの岩場、ポール=ドモワ》、カミーユ・ピサロ《ヴァランジュヴィル、アンゴ館の果樹園と鶏》、アルフレッド・シスレー《ブージヴァル》、そしてゴッホの《ポプラ林の中の二人》の4種類の表紙で登場。何冊でも集めたくなる美しいデザイン。各1430円（税込）。

トートバッグ

トートバッグは、シスレーの《ブージヴァル》がプリントされたオレンジ、フェルディナント・ホドラー《聖なる時間》がプリントされたパープル、フレデリック・バジール《キョウチクトウ（メリックのテラス）》がプリントされたピンクの3種類（各税込3300円）。刺繍雑貨ブランド「ito&」とコラボ商品（税込4290円）には、ゴッホの《ポプラ林の中の二人》とシンシナティ美術館のロゴが刺繍されている。トートバッグ専門ブランド「ROOTOTE」とコラボした「トールフラット」（税込4180円）には、《ブージヴァル》が大胆にプリントされ、外側にはビニールのポケットもついている。

クリアポーチ、ボンフィン キーホルダー

実用性のある大きめサイズのクリアポーチ（税込1760円）は、鮮やかで目を引くカラーリングがおしゃれ。リボンに絵画がプリントされたボンフィンキーホルダー（税込880円）をジッパー部分につけてカスタマイズするのもおすすめ。

かまわぬ てぬぐい、豆団扇

てぬぐいブランド「かまわぬ」とのコラボレーションとして、てぬぐい（税込4620円）と豆団扇（税込3300円）がラインアップ。豆団扇は、表面にてぬぐいを貼った小ぶりなサイズの竹の団扇で、持ち運びにも便利。実用性とデザイン性を兼ね備えたてぬぐいで、アートを暮らしに取り入れよう。

アンリ・シャルパンティエ ガトー・キュイ・アソート

洋菓子ブランド「アンリ・シャルパンティエ」とのコラボレーション。バジールの《キョウチクトウ（メリックのテラス）》をモチーフにしたオリジナルスイーツ缶は、食べ終わってからも小物や雑貨を収納して飾りたい美しさ。3024円（税込）。

おはじきふうシール

丸型、花型、ハート型に切り取られた絵画が、ぷっくりと立体的になったおはじきふうシール。小さなサイズ感も可愛らしく、ユニークなお土産としても喜ばれそう。990円（税込）。

スマホマグネットケース

MagSafe対応のスマホマグネットケース。iPhoneの裏面に貼りつけるだけで、お気に入りの絵画をいつでも身近に携帯できる。ケースにはカード1枚を収納可能。2860円（税込）。

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Alliance Media Partners ( AMP ) has boarded worldwide sales on Modem , a timely techno horror tapping into the contemporary human obsession with digital connectivity, ahead of the AFM .

The picture unfolds against the backdrop of a family digital detox vacation in a house in a Swedish forest which takes a terrifying turn when a teenager discovers an old modem and unwittingly awakens a dormant, sadistic demon when it is fired up.

The sinister presence torments the family, and when their two-year-old suddenly vanishes, fear spirals into hysteria and paranoia as the family confronts a terrifying force that has turned their connected world against them.

Related Stories

Hot Armando Iannucci Package Heading To AFM With James McAvoy, Alicia Vikander & Taron Egerton - The Dish

Prestige International Pictures Boards SXSW Mexican Teen Body Horror 'Fifteen' - AFM

Modem is the directorial feature debut of Tim James Brown, who also wrote the screenplay, and stars Josh Burdett, Amanda Renberg, Nika Tallroth, Frederik Gunnarsson, Ylva Loof, Henrik Lundstrom.

Watch on Deadline

“What makes Modem so intense is that it plays on the paranoia of technology – a paranormal stalker voyeuristically preying on its victims through their own digital devices. You can’t see it – it sees you ,” said Brown.

The award-winning film has played at Raindance , the Stockholm City Film Festival and at the New York International Film Awards, and will make its market debut at the AFM.

AMP’s Head of Sales and Acquisitions Anthony Buckner negotiated the deal with Jonathan Sadler on behalf of the filmmakers.

‘Modem is exactly the kind of high-concept horror we’re excited to bring to the international market,” said Buckner.

“It taps into a universal modern-day obsession with being online and turns something we rely on every day into a source of genuine terror. With its compelling premise and chillingly relevant themes, we believe the film has strong potential to connect with young audiences worldwide.”
