article_text:
In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture. But that shouldn’t be the case.

While a documentary can win its own Oscar, reshape the cultural conversation and become one of the defining films of its era, these nonfiction feature films have been excluded from the top category meant to honor the year’s best filmmaking. When the Academy expanded the Best Picture lineup from five to 10 after the snub of “The Dark Knight” (2008), the press release led with the possibility of a documentary getting recognized. That has yet to happen … perhaps until now?

That assumption is finally being tested this season with “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s nonfiction sensation about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Acclaim and box office success are raising the possibility that a documentary could finally break one of the Academy’s longest-standing barriers. If it earns a nomination, the achievement would be historic. But it would also raise an uncomfortable question: Why did it take this long?

To celebrate this potential historic nomination, Variety is ranking the 20 films that should have received a best picture nomination in the past 40 years.

The films mentioned here span genres, styles and subjects, from the pursuit of an NBA dream to a high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers, from a confrontation with Indonesia’s history of mass killing to a real-time account of Edward Snowden’s revelations.

You can blame the Academy at large for some of these omissions; others tie directly to the Documentary Branch itself, which snubbed many of them in its own category.

If “You Can See Everything” finally breaks through, it will undoubtedly have earned its place in history. But it should not have been the first. Many others from this very year could also be deemed worthy, such as “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” and “Naza.”

Read the list below.

Honorable mentions : “An Inconvenient Truth” (2006); “Senna” (2010); “The Act of Killing” (2012); “Apollo 11″ (2019)

Daughters (2024) Image Credit: Courtesy of Sundance Institute Angela Patton and Natalie Rae’s “Daughters” follows four girls preparing for a father-daughter dance inside a Washington, D.C., prison as part of a fatherhood program Patton helped build. The filmmakers’ choice to focus on the girls’ anticipation, anger and longing is its strongest element. It carries the film toward a dance sequence of almost unbearable tenderness. It won both the Audience Award and the Festival Favorite prize at Sundance, then made the documentary shortlist only to miss the nomination at the 2025 ceremony. Few films that year said more about love under impossible conditions.

Man on Wire (2008) James Marsh’s “Man on Wire” reconstructs Philippe Petit’s 1974 high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers. Through interviews, archival footage and recreations, Marsh builds a structure as a model for any good movie heist. “Man on Wire” won the documentary Oscar at the 2009 ceremony, and its success lives on, demonstrating how effectively a nonfiction film could deliver the pleasures of a caper.

O.J.: Made in America (2016) Image Credit: ESPN There are strong feelings about whether or not Ezra Edelman’s Oscar winner is, in fact, a documentary feature, but it’s included nonetheless. Edelman’s nearly eight-hour “O.J.: Made in America” is an expansive examination of race, celebrity, policing and the American justice system, using the life of O.J. Simpson as a lens through which to understand the country’s social and cultural divisions. What begins as a portrait of an athlete becomes a sweeping account of Los Angeles and the forces that shaped one of the most consequential public dramas of the modern era. The documentary feature Oscar winner’s format also exposed the boundaries of the category. Its recognition prompted renewed scrutiny of how the Academy treats multipart nonfiction projects, contributing to subsequent eligibility changes concerning episodic work. Whatever the debate over its classification, the filmmaking is extraordinary. Its scope exceeds that of most narrative features.

Won’t You Be My Neighbor? (2018) Image Credit: Everett Collection / Everett Colllection Morgan Neville’s portrait of television icon Fred Rogers became the highest-grossing biographical documentary of its time and became a sensation for all of us who grew up with the prolific figure. Rather than canonize its subject, Oscar winner Neville (“20 Feet From Stardom”) examines the radical patience behind “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood” and the quiet conviction that children deserved to be taken seriously. The film made the documentary shortlist but, shockingly, missed a nomination at the 2019 ceremony, a snub that still stings. Few films that year moved audiences so completely, in any category.

Flee (2021) Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s “Flee” uses animation to tell the story of Amin, an Afghan refugee who reveals the full extent of his childhood and his journey to safety. The decision to use the animation medium for the testimony allows Amin to revisit traumatic memories while preserving his anonymity, creating a visual language for experiences that would be difficult to reconstruct. “Flee” made Oscar history by becoming the first film nominated for documentary feature, international feature and animated feature in the same year. It lost in all three categories, and best picture remained out of reach. Rasmussen’s film is a reminder that nonfiction is not confined to one visual language or storytelling tradition.

The Look of Silence (2014) Image Credit: Getty Many will argue I chose the wrong Joshua Oppenheimer film, and that “The Act of Killing” is more worthy of a spot than its companion piece. That a filmmaker’s work can spark such a debate is itself a mark of genius. “The Look of Silence” approaches Indonesia’s 1965-66 mass killings through an optometrist whose brother was murdered during the violence. Oppenheimer resists the conventions of a historical exposé, allowing pauses and glances to communicate what his subjects refuse to say. The film landed a documentary feature nomination but lost to “Amy.”

Cameraperson (2016) Image Credit: Courtesy of Sundance Film Festival Kirsten Johnson spent decades as a documentary cinematographer, filming subjects in war zones, hospitals and interview rooms. With “Cameraperson,” she assembled fragments from that career into a moving essay about the ethics of looking and the emotional toll of bearing witness. The doc branch failed to nominate “Cameraperson,” a shocking omission for a work so widely admired for its originality. Johnson’s 2020 follow-up, “Dick Johnson Is Dead,” a playful and heartbreaking reckoning with her father’s decline, that could just as easily have claimed this spot.

13th (2016) Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix Ava DuVernay’s “13th” examines the connection between the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery, and the rise of mass incarceration in the United States. Through interviews with scholars, activists and politicians, alongside archival footage, DuVernay builds an argument about the enduring relationship between race and the criminal justice system. Rather than treating the amendment as a historical endpoint, she traces how its language became a blueprint for systems of control, and presenting a complex history with clarity and urgency. “13th” opened the 2016 New York Film Festival and landed a documentary feature nom, losing to “O.J.: Made in America.” A decade later, DuVernay returned to NYFF with the equally urgent “14th,” the festival’s 2026 closing night film, which Netflix will also release.

Dear Zachary: A Letter to a Son About His Father (2008) No documentary has made me cry more than the one about a baby named Zachary. Kurt Kuenne began “Dear Zachary” as a film for the infant son of his murdered best friend, Andrew Bagby. And what starts as a tribute built from home videos, photographs and memories becomes a devastating account of grief, family and a legal system that fails those seeking justice. Kuenne is not a detached observer. As events unfold, the film’s purpose changes, and its structure takes on a force no viewer can anticipate. Kuenne’s mid-film narration is something your heart can never properly prepare for. Nonetheless, the documentary branch passed on “Dear Zachary.” It remains one of the clearest examples of why documentaries deserve to be considered among the year’s best films, not merely the year’s best documentaries.

Exit Through the Gift Shop (2010) Banksy’s “Exit Through the Gift Shop” makes uncertainty part of the moviewatching experience. Is the film documenting an absurd art-world spectacle, manufacturing one or doing both at once? Banksy never provides a definitive answer, and the film’s refusal to settle the question gives it life. “Exit Through the Gift Shop” earned a documentary feature nom, losing to “Inside Job.” Moreover, it challenged the assumption that documentaries must present a distinction between observer and participant.

I Am Not Your Negro (2016) Image Credit: Courtesy of TIFF Raoul Peck’s Oscar-nominated “I Am Not Your Negro” takes James Baldwin’s unfinished manuscript about Medgar Evers, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. and transforms it into a searing cinematic essay on race and America. Samuel L. Jackson narrates Baldwin’s words, with the film’s force coming from the collision between the writer’s observations and a country that still refuses to reckon with its past. It’s sheer brilliance, and always timely.

Three Identical Strangers (2018) Image Credit: Courtesy of Sundance Film Festival Tim Wardle’s film opens as a feel-good reunion of triplets separated at birth and curdles into an account of a secret psychological study that treated infants as test subjects. Wardle controls the revelations with the discipline of a thriller, letting each turn leave the viewer shocked before the next is revealed. Like “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?,” it was shortlisted and then passed over entirely by the documentary branch. Its story of nature, nurture and institutional betrayal deserved a much wider stage.

Citizenfour (2014) Image Credit: Courtesy of The Weinstein Company Laura Poitras’ “Citizenfour” puts viewers inside a Hong Kong hotel room while Edward Snowden meets journalists and begins revealing classified information about government surveillance. Poitras allows conversations to develop in real time, building suspense through the simple act of watching history unfold. “Citizenfour” won the documentary Oscar at the 2015 ceremony, but no best picture heat would ensue.

Searching for Sugar Man (2012) Malik Bendjelloul’s “Searching for Sugar Man” chases the ghost of Rodriguez, a Detroit musician whose albums vanished in America but became anthems in apartheid-era South Africa, where fans knew nothing about the man behind the music. By my estimation, it’s the single standout nonfiction film of its decade. Bendjelloul builds the mystery like a detective story, with an emotional payoff that feels almost too extraordinary to be true. Rodriguez’s incredible songs carry a story about fame, obscurity and the strange ways art outlives the circumstances of its making. Oscar voters handed it the documentary prize in 2013. Nobody mounted a best picture push for a film that had already proven it could hold a broad audience in its palm. Bendjelloul died in 2014 at 36, but the joyous discovery he left behind is well intact.

Grizzly Man (2005) Image Credit: ©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection Werner Herzog’s “Grizzly Man” begins with footage shot by Timothy Treadwell, a self-appointed protector of Alaskan grizzlies who was killed by one of the animals he sought to defend. Herzog’s narration becomes a film unto itself, challenging Treadwell’s romantic vision of the wilderness. The footage is funny, unnerving and devastating, sometimes within the same frame. Few filmmakers have turned a real-life tragedy into a philosophical inquiry so effectively without losing sight of the person at its center. Unfortunately, this was yet another victim of the doc branch’s allergy to mainstream and successful films, even though it’s widely considered among Herzog’s most celebrated works.

Stories We Tell (2012) Image Credit: National Board of Canada Sarah Polley’s “Stories We Tell” is an investigation into her own family history and becomes a remarkably intricate exploration of memory, and the fragile relationship between personal truth and the stories people preserve. Polley interviews relatives and friends, reconstructing family moments with its most effective moments being best experienced without advance knowledge of the revelations it shows. “Stories We Tell” was snubbed for the documentary Oscar, let alone best picture. That omission is particularly striking given Polley’s command of structure and her willingness to question the very conventions on which documentary filmmaking depends.

Bowling for Columbine (2002) Image Credit: ©United Artists/Courtesy Everett Collection Michael Moore turned the Columbine High School massacre into a mirror for America to see. “Bowling for Columbine” interrogates America’s relationship with guns, violence and fear, mixing interviews, archival footage and Moore’s confrontational on-camera presence into an argument that dared audiences to fight back. Few releases of 2002 commanded that attention. The Writers Guild made it the first documentary to win its original screenplay prize, and the Academy followed with the documentary Oscar, where Moore’s “shame on you, Mr. Bush” speech became the most talked-about moment of the night (and history).

Hoop Dreams (1994) Image Credit: ©Fine Line Features/Courtesy Everett Collection No documentary snub remains quite as painful as the Academy’s failure to recognize Steve James’ “Hoop Dreams.” Over five years, James followed Chicago teenagers William Gates and Arthur Agee as they pursued basketball dreams that promised an escape from poverty. The result is a nearly three-hour American epic about race, class, family and the machinery that turns young athletes into commodities. Critics embraced the film as one of the year’s finest, regardless of genre. The Academy’s documentary branch, however, failed to nominate it, prompting widespread criticism and contributing to voting changes in the documentary nomination process. Interestingly, “Hoop Dreams” managed to receive an Oscar nomination for film editing, but best picture was likely an even more distant possibility.

The Thin Blue Line (1988) Image Credit: Courtesy of Miramax Films Errol Morris’ investigation into the 1976 killing of a Dallas police officer did something few doc films hope to do: It helped free an innocent man. Randall Dale Adams was released from prison within a year of the film’s debut, after Morris’ interviews exposed the holes in the case against him. Its stylized reenactments, Philip Glass score and noir structure reinvented the nonfiction form in many ways. Once again, the doc branch had other plans, with a snub measured just as scandalous in its moment as “Hoop Dreams” would be six years later. Leaving out the film that changed how documentaries are made is indefensible.

Paris is Burning (1990) Jennie Livingston’s “Paris Is Burning” documents Harlem’s ballroom scene in the late 1980s, where Black and Latino queer performers built houses, families and an entire vocabulary of survival in the face of poverty, racism and the AIDS crisis. Its subjects, including Pepper LaBeija, Dorian Corey and Venus Xtravaganza, are among the most vivid figures nonfiction cinema has captured. The film won the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance yet was snubbed by the Academy’s documentary branch at the 1992 ceremony. Decades later, its influence has been felt in artistic achievements such as television’s “Pose,” “RuPaul’s Drag Race” and the mainstream itself.

article_text:
El director de Ida y Cold War reconstruye los pasos del escritor alemán a su país tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial, con una Sandra Hüller extraordinaria.

Luego de varios años, Pawel Pawlikowski volvió a poner en tela de juicio las heridas de Europa con Fatherland . La película transcurre y nos enseña el regreso de Thomas Mann a Alemania, dividida en Occidental y Oriental. El director polaco construye un drama austero sobre el exilio, la identidad y las contradicciones de una familia atravesada por la tragedia (que también se hace presente durante el viaje).

Con apenas 82 minutos de duración, el film demuestra que no necesita extenderse para abordar cuestiones políticas, culturales y personales . Sin embargo, su apuesta por la solemnidad y el diálogo constante puede volverla algo distante por momentos, ya que no ahonda en los sentimientos de sus personajes, si no en la palabra de cada uno de ellos.

¿En qué se basa la cinta?

La historia transcurre en 1949, cuando Thomas Mann ( Hanns Zischler ), ganador del Premio Nobel de Literatura y autor de La montaña mágica , regresa a Alemania después de años de exilio. Acompañado por su hija Erika ( Sandra Hüller ), viaja entre Frankfurt, bajo influencia occidental, y Weimar, situada en el sector controlado por los soviéticos.

El cineasta nos pone el foco en como el escritor es recibido como una figura de enorme prestigio, aunque su regreso también despierta cuestionamientos , hasta de su propia familia. Para algunos, haber abandonado el país durante el nazismo lo convierte en un traidor; para otros, su presencia representa una oportunidad para reconstruir la identidad cultural alemana después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial.

Mann se “enfrenta” a un país que ya no reconoce y a una sociedad que intenta reconstruirse sin haber resuelto por completo sus responsabilidades históricas. Su recorrido también deja al descubierto las tensiones de una familia marcada por los desencuentros y las heridas que nunca terminaron de cerrar .

Te puede interesar

Reseña de “Entrega al límite”: Alan Ritchson y Owen Wilson forman una gran dupla que sabe dar lecciones y no solo a los golpes

Reseña de “Wildwood: Bosque Salvaje”, una aventura de magia y amor familiar

Sandra Hüller, la destacada de la película

Aunque el personaje de Zischler es el centro del relato, Erika, de la mano de Hüller , adquiere un protagonismo fundamental. No es solo la hija que acompaña al escritor: también es su conductora, intérprete y asistente. Como también, es una mujer que no se deja avasallar y no permite que la pisoteen.

La interpretación combina contención, ironía y frustración, mientras deja entrever el desgaste de una relación marcada por el afecto y el resentimiento con su pasado.

Zischler también consigue darle dimensión a un hombre que parece protegerse detrás de su prestigio intelectual. Su Mann es una figura sumamente admirada, pero en la soledad de lo familiar es un padre distante y que no muestra sus sentimientos (hasta el final).

La relación entre ambos personajes es la que marca buena parte de la película y evita que el recorrido histórico por una Alemania devastada se convierta únicamente en una sucesión de discursos y encuentros diplomáticos.

El blanco y negro como sello del director

Como ya había sucedido en las mencionadas cintas, Pawlikowski vuelve a trabajar con el blanco y negro y un encuadre de proporciones clásicas. La fotografía de Łukasz Żal convierte las ciudades destruidas, los hoteles y los espacios institucionales en escenarios cargados de significado.

La puesta en escena es uno de los mayores aciertos de Fatherland . Los personajes aparecen muchas veces pequeños frente a espacios inmensos, una decisión que refuerza la sensación de impotencia ante el peso de la historia. Las ruinas no funcionan solamente como parte de la reconstrucción de época: también representan las dificultades de reparar una sociedad moralmente devastada.

La pregunta que intenta responder la cinta

La película plantea una pregunta que atraviesa toda su historia: ¿es posible reconstruir una patria después de que sus propios habitantes hayan contribuido a destruirla? Pawlikowski no ofrece respuestas sencillas y evita convertir a Mann en un héroe sin contradicciones. Su mirada es rigurosa y elegante, aunque por momentos demasiado académica. La brevedad del relato juega a favor de su concisión, pero también deja algunos aspectos de la familia Mann apenas sugeridos.

¿Vale la pena mirarla?

La producción es una propuesta sólida, visualmente extraordinaria y sostenida por dos actuaciones de gran nivel. Pawlikowski demuestra una dominio de la puesta en escena y su capacidad para encontrar historias personales dentro de los grandes acontecimientos históricos. Si bien por momentos la cinta puede ser tediosa y hasta generar incomodidad en el espectador, siempre muestra una mirada diferente.

El resultado es un drama elegante y melancólico que encuentra en Sandra Hüller una de sus mayores fortalezas y confirma que, para Pawlikowski, las ruinas de Europa siguen siendo un territorio fértil para explorar las contradicciones humanas.

De la mano de MUBI y MACO, la cinta se estrena el próximo 26 de octubre.

Calificación: 7.5/10.

title_original: Crítica | Antártida (2026): quando a investigação esquece a vítima
editorial_title_zh: 影评 | 《南极洲》（2026）：当调查遗忘了受害者
editorial_excerpt_zh: 尽管演员阵容作出了努力，这部长片仍将女主角的创伤简化为一个引不起兴趣的谜团，并浪费了在极地基地禁闭所带来的紧张感。文章《影评 | 《南极洲》（2026）：当调查遗忘了受害者》首先出现在 Cinema com Rapadura 上。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "尽管演员阵容作出了努力，这部长片仍将女主角的创伤简化为一个引不起兴趣的谜团，并浪费了在极地基地禁闭所带来的紧张感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一座冰层中孤立的研究站是犯罪与调查题材电影的理想场景。远离任何援助，并且必须继续与一个潜在的侵害者共享空间，本可蓄积悬疑感并让朝夕相处变得令人窒息。《南极洲》对这种处境的利用却极其有限。随着叙事集中于查明伊内斯（玛丽娜·鲁伊·巴博萨 饰）遭强暴的责任人，这个角色逐渐失去了存在感，创伤也几乎沦为了推动谜团发展的纯粹工具。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "副指挥官伊丽莎白（安德烈娅·贝特朗 饰）作为负责接手调查的人物出场，她审问着潜在的罪魁祸首，而剧本则抛出了基地成员间的种种秘密和新的暴力处境。然而，这些发现的严重性并未配得上相应的戏剧构建。这些都是关于那些电影几乎没让我们去了解过的人物的揭露，缺乏充分的发展，以至于这些发现无法引发惊异或触动公众的感知。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "克劳迪娅·茹文（Cláudia Jouvin）的剧本试图通过汇集各种不断累积、反而损害了深度的虐待与大男子主义表现来扩大批判。例如，玛丽娜（莱昂德拉·利尔 饰）的过去之所以重要，是因为它涉及另一个侵害者同样身处基地的虐待案件，但在它本可承载的分量面前，它得到的关注却小得不成比例。对话试图通过解释冲突和意图来弥补这种仓促，就好像让信息变得清晰就能替代去切实感受后果所带来的冲击一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我们看到伊内斯被边缘化并囚禁起来，而其他人则在讨论这起犯罪时，伊内斯的情况显得更加成问题——她不再主导关于自身遭遇的视角。其他角色代她发言，叙事对这些对话的关注远胜于对她情绪状态的关注。这种处境本身本可揭露受害者甚至如何被声称在帮助她的人剥夺自主权，但电影对这种可能性的探索却少之又少，调查在没有将她的缺席当成一个问题的情况下继续推进。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "即便有着这样的侧重点，这个谜团也同样站不住脚。迟迟不去看监控录像，随之又缺乏获取画面的主动性，这只是剧本刻意拖延答案的努力的一个例子。支线浪漫情节和新的威胁为本就超载的情节增添了歧路，却没有任何东西能让这场搜寻变得更为扣人心弦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有一点很突出，那就是对雪景和极地风光的重现，在大多数时候都颇具说服力。然而，布鲁诺·萨法迪（Bruno Safadi）的导演手法对这一场景的利用却微乎其微。镜头几乎无时无刻不在记录表演，不让我们去了解这个基地，也感受不到共享那些空间的别扭。剪辑通过用外部的冰雪画面打断激烈的对话，突显了这种距离感——这些重复的转场不过是事件之间泛泛的暂停，并未能强化禁闭感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "演员们依然在努力从素材中寻找某种人性，尤其是安德烈娅·贝特朗、莱昂德拉·利尔和拉扎罗·拉莫斯。而玛丽娜·鲁伊·巴博萨则哪怕在空间被不断压缩的情况下依然撑起了伊内斯这个角色。尽管表演前后一致，但单凭这些演绎却无法创造出场景所缺失的连贯性与情感分量。一种奇怪的感觉油然而生：观众仿佛在看着优秀的演员试图赋予那些被剧本保持空洞的人物以生命。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "顶着探讨对女性暴力的期许，《南极洲》对叙事进行了一种削弱自身批判力度的编排。而作为一部“谁干的”（whodunnit）电影，该片既缺乏谜团的力度，最重要的是，缺乏利用布景和孤立状态来营造紧张感的能力。所有人都想弄清伊内斯身上发生了什么，但电影几乎懒得去问她现在过得怎么样。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Apesar do esforço do elenco, longa reduz o trauma de sua protagonista a um mistério pouco envolvente e desperdiça a tensão do confinamento numa base polar."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Uma estação de pesquisa isolada no gelo é o cenário ideal para um longa de crime e investigação. A distância de qualquer ajuda e a necessidade de continuar dividindo espaços com um possível agressor poderiam alimentar o suspense e tornar a convivência insuportável. “ Antártida ” aproveita bem pouco dessa situação. article_text:
Apesar do esforço do elenco, longa reduz o trauma de sua protagonista a um mistério pouco envolvente e desperdiça a tensão do confinamento numa base polar.

Uma estação de pesquisa isolada no gelo é o cenário ideal para um longa de crime e investigação. A distância de qualquer ajuda e a necessidade de continuar dividindo espaços com um possível agressor poderiam alimentar o suspense e tornar a convivência insuportável. “ Antártida ” aproveita bem pouco dessa situação. À medida que a narrativa se concentra em identificar o responsável pelo estupro de Inês (Marina Ruy Barbosa), a personagem perde presença, e o trauma passa a servir quase exclusivamente à movimentação do mistério.

A subcomandante Elisabeth (Andrea Beltrão) surge como a figura responsável por assumir a investigação, interrogando os possíveis culpados enquanto o roteiro apresenta segredos e novas situações de violência entre os integrantes da base. A gravidade dessas descobertas, porém, não encontra uma construção dramática à altura. Trata-se de revelações sobre pessoas que o filme mal nos permitiu conhecer, sem desenvolvimento suficiente para que as descobertas provoquem surpresa ou mexam com a percepção do público.

O roteiro de Cláudia Jouvin tenta ampliar a denúncia reunindo diferentes manifestações de abuso e machismo que se acumulam e prejudicam o aprofundamento. O passado de Marina (Leandra Leal), por exemplo, é significativo por se tratar de outro caso de abuso cujo agressor também está na base, mas recebe uma atenção desproporcionalmente pequena diante do peso que poderia ter. Os diálogos procuram compensar essa pressa explicando os conflitos e as intenções, como se deixar a mensagem clara substituísse o impacto de sentir as consequências de fato.

O caso de Inês se mostra ainda mais problemático ao vermos a personagem sendo mantida distante e enclausurada enquanto os demais discutem o crime — ela deixa de conduzir a perspectiva sobre o que lhe aconteceu. Outros personagens falam por ela, e a narrativa acompanha essas conversas com mais interesse do que acompanha seu estado emocional. A situação por si só já poderia expor a maneira como uma vítima é privada de autonomia mesmo por quem afirma ajudá-la, mas o filme pouco explora essa possibilidade, e a investigação prossegue sem que sua ausência se torne uma questão.

Mesmo com essa prioridade, o mistério também não se sustenta com firmeza. A demora em considerar as câmeras de segurança, seguida da falta de iniciativa para obter as imagens, é apenas um exemplo do esforço do roteiro para adiar respostas. Romances acessórios e novas ameaças acrescentam desvios a uma trama já sobrecarregada, e nada chega a tornar a busca mais intrigante.

Algo que se destaca é a recriação da neve e da paisagem polar, que convence na maior parte do tempo. A direção de Bruno Safadi, contudo, tira pouco proveito desse cenário. A câmera foca quase a todo momento no registro das atuações, sem nos permitir conhecer a base ou sentir o desconforto de compartilhar aqueles espaços. A montagem acentua essa distância ao interromper conversas intensas com imagens externas do gelo — transições repetidas que funcionam como meras pausas genéricas entre acontecimentos, sem intensificar a sensação de confinamento.

O elenco ainda se esforça para encontrar algo humano no material, sobretudo Andrea Beltrão, Leandra Leal e Lázaro Ramos. Já Marina Ruy Barbosa sustenta Inês mesmo com o espaço progressivamente reduzido. Apesar de consistentes, as interpretações não conseguem criar sozinhas a continuidade e o peso emocional que faltam às cenas. Surge uma sensação estranha de acompanhar bons atores tentando dar vida a figuras que o roteiro mantém vazias.

Com a pretensão de discutir a violência contra a mulher, “Antártida” organiza sua narrativa de um modo que enfraquece a própria denúncia. Já como um filme whodunnit, falta força ao mistério e, acima de tudo, capacidade de usar a ambientação e o isolamento a favor da tensão. Todos querem descobrir o que aconteceu com Inês, mas o filme mal se preocupa em perguntar como ela está.

article_text:
Tony Kaye , the British director of “ American History X ” and “Detachment,” will direct “Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow?,” a short running five minutes that blends documentary with reality drama and plays out among the giant monster sculptures installed across Leicester, England.

Hiu Man Chan, a film entrepreneur and academic in creative industries at De Montfort University, is producing. The project will pair Kaye with up-and-coming actors and filmmakers from the university and Leicester’s wider creative scene, and the production is taking an experimental, collaborative route.

Related Stories

Spotify Has Removed 50 Million AI Slop Tracks From Recommendations This Year

The narrative will take shape around the chosen cast and participants, with the camera catching chance encounters and real human experiences as the film asks whether people can come to understand and love each other across their differences. The shoot commences on Friday. Louis Lingjaerde (“Vipers”) is the cinematographer.

The short will take its setting from Leicester Monsters, a downtown program run by BID Leicester that has placed oversized creatures on the city’s streets and in its public spaces to coax visitors into exploring the center. Bristol-based Designs in Air installed the monsters.

“Forty years ago, I made a commercial for solid fuel in which a dog, a cat and a mouse kissed each other in front of a real coal fire, to the music of ‘Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow.’ I’ve never forgotten that image,” Kaye said. “Now, with the Leicester Monsters movie, I find myself returning to the same idea. Perhaps the universe is the real coal fire, and we are all just animals gathered around it, trying to work out how to love one another. The question is as simple as it is impossible: how can we all get along, forever?”

Leicester is often described as one of the most diverse cities in the U.K. The film will use that mix, with giant creatures popping up around town as a surreal backdrop, to probe the pull between difference and belonging, and between freedom and commitment.

“I am passionate about the most important human feeling – love – in storytelling, as well as packaging unique projects like this to challenge conventional filmmaking. I look forward to this creative journey with Tony, one of Britain’s greatest talents, and to put the city of Leicester in motion,” Chan said.

Kaye’s first feature, 1998’s “American History X,” tackled racism and redemption and earned Edward Norton an Oscar nomination for best actor. His 2011 film “Detachment,” starring Adrien Brody, took two prizes at the Deauville American Film Festival – the Critics’ Award and the Revelation Prize – and won the Tokyo International Film Festival ’s Best Artistic Contribution Award. He also directed the 2006 documentary “Lake of Fire.”

The release of “American History X” was famously fraught. Kaye fell out with New Line Cinema and Norton over the edit, and the version that reached theaters, which Norton had a hand in cutting, ran longer than Kaye’s original 95-minute cut. Kaye spent around $100,000 on dozens of ads in the Hollywood trades, Variety among them, some of which attacked Norton and the studio. The Directors Guild of America turned down his request to swap his directing credit for a pseudonym, among them “Humpty Dumpty.” Kaye later sued the guild and New Line for $200 million, a case that was dismissed in 2000.

Kaye returned to the saga in “Humpty Dumpty X,” a 74-minute documentary built from camcorder footage he shot during the dispute, including phone calls with studio executives. The film, which also features Marlon Brando, world premiered in the Spotlight Documentary section of this year’s Tribeca Festival.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Production has wrapped on under-the-radar “Gen Z music thriller” Dead At 27 , starring Selma Blair ( Cruel Intentions ), Sierra McCormick ( American Horror Stories ), Logan Miller ( Escape Room ) and Dylan Playfair ( Letterkenny) .

The film will feature acting and music from recording artists Iann Dior, Tommy Genesis and Kya (Bludnymph) Hansen. K. Asher Levin directs.

Described as a “hallucinatory descent into the dark side of music and pop culture, Dead at 27 explores our modern addiction to fame, validation, and the spectacle of its own destruction…When a reclusive pop icon resurfaces with a dangerously addictive new sound, a generation of fans falls under her spell.”

Related Stories

Selma Blair Charged With Assaults On Cop & Nurse After Airplane Incident

Selma Blair Announces 'Hineni' Doc About Antisemitism After She Was "Erased" Over Islamophobic Comments

The film was written by Levin and Zack Imbrogno and produced by Levin, Ashleigh Snead, Henry Boger (Freefall Films), and Michael May. Executive producers are Selma Blair, Iann Dior, Andile Ndlovu and Jasmine Pears, with Ronnie Exley and Jeremy Ross serving as co-executive producers. Paul Yurick, Adam Stillwell and Nick Daue are co-producers.

Watch on Deadline

The film features a full original soundtrack written by Levin and Theresa Wayman, featuring performances by cast members and recording artists Tommy Genesis, Iann Dior, Kya (Bludnymph) Hansen and Logan Miller.

The film was shot by cinematographer Andy Chen and edited by Alex Rodriguez ( Children of Men, Y Tu Mamá También ) and Raul Toledo.

The film marks the latest collaboration between Levin and Snead, who first worked together as producers on Adam Egypt Mortimer’s Fantastic Fest title Pathetic Fallacy , alongside veteran genre producer Steven Schneider.

Blair is repped by Berlandi Nussbaum & Reitzas, Oren Segal and Jill Fritzo PR. McCormick is represented by Innovative Artists, Management Production Entertainment, and The Nord Group. Miller is represented by Paradigm, Atlas and Hirsch Wallerstein Hayum Matlof and Fishman. Playfair is repped by Carrie Wheeler Entertainment Group and 3 Arts Entertainment.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Terry Sanders has finished his latest project On Rescuing Democracy and the Rule of Law .

Two-time Oscar winner Sanders writes and directs the documentary. It explores the challenges and threats that established democracies, including the U.S., are facing and tells the story of the people who became involved with the Central and East European Law Initiative (CEELI) after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

The doc tells the story of how more than 5,000 American lawyers, judges and legal experts became involved with CEELI, which was a pro bono initiative that provided technical legal assistance to former Soviet Bloc countries. Its work included helping to rewrite the constitutions of these countries, reform court systems, and adopt democratic rule of law principles.

Related Stories

HBO's Harry Potter Casts Its Ghosts, Sorting Hat & Fat Lady On Halloween Eve

Forest Whitaker Joins Rachid Bouchareb's 'Boomerang Atomic' As EP Ahead Of DOC NYC Screening

Former U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has said: “In my judgment, CEELI is the most effective voluntary legal assistance initiative in history.”

Watch on Deadline

Veteran filmmaker Sanders is co-head of the American Film Foundation, which produced On Rescuing Democracy and the Rule of Law . His earlier work includes producing Oscar-winning short A Time Out of War and co-producing Maya Lin: A Strong Clear Vision , which won the Best Documentary Feature Oscar.

The team behind the new film said it will document how populist surges have softened some countries’ resolve to protect established democratic rule of law, and how the U.S. experienced a violent assault on the Capitol on January 6, 2021.

Sanders explained to Deadline his the 33-minute doc is in three parts. It starts at the end of WWII and the Cold War, before taking in the fall of the Berlin Wall and rise of democracy in former Soviet Bloc countries. It goes on to take in events including January 6, before looking at the rise of authoritarianism and concluding with segments on the situation today and where we head next.

On Rescuing Democracy and the Rule of Law has contributions from Homer Moyer, co-founder of CEELI, Mark Ellis, Executive Director of the International Bar Association, Betsy Andersen, former Executive Director of the World Justice Project as well as Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O’Connor and historian Corey Brettschneider.
